items.title: CDC benchmark stand: outboxx vs Debezium
items.body:
Closes #42.

Adds a reproducible local stand to benchmark outboxx against Debezium on the same PostgreSQL WAL, so the "outboxx beats Debezium" observation can be checked fairly instead of eyeballed from a screenshot.

- Stand under `tests/load/`: Postgres → CDC (outboxx | Debezium) → Kafka, with Prometheus + Grafana + cAdvisor.
- outboxx builds from the local checkout, so local changes are what gets measured (not GitHub `main`).
- Debezium is tuned for throughput (2 GB heap, enlarged batches) so the comparison isn't a strawman; its config lives in the repo.
- Consistent `debezium` naming across topics, services, and the dashboard.
- README throughput row updated to the measured run.

Numbers are indicative (single local run on Apple M1): outboxx ~150k evt/s vs Debezium ~90k, at a fraction of the CPU and memory. Not a controlled multi-run A/B yet.

items.title: Record FastAPI-Startkit benchmark results (SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL) + config fixes
items.body:
## Summary

Records measured **FastAPI-Startkit** benchmark results into the README results tables for **SQLite, PostgreSQL 17, and MySQL 8** (Tests 1–3, operations A–K), per task #608. Includes the correctness fixes required to actually run on PG/MySQL.

Branched off current `master` (PR #5 is already merged, so this is a fresh PR, not a push to the merged branch).

## README changes

- Adds a **FastAPI-Startkit** column to all 9 per-DB results tables (SQLite / PostgreSQL / MySQL × Tests 1–3) with measured rows/sec for each operation + geometric mean.
- **Existing ORM rows and the "Best" column are unchanged.** FastAPI-Startkit was measured separately (different machine/run, sequential execution) and is **not** factored into "Best".
- Adds a methodology note + a MySQL footnote.

## Code changes (enumerated for delta review)

1. **`models.py` — explicit connection `url` for Postgres/MySQL (correctness).** `PostgresConfig`/`MySQLConfig` ship a bogus default `url=sqlite+aiosqlite:///…`, and `build_url()` prefers `url` over host/port — so PG/MySQL **silently fell back to SQLite**. Without this the merged benchmark misreports PG/MySQL. *(Same bug is in the upstream-contribution branch — must be fixed before any upstream PR.)*
2. **`models.py` — wide-model float columns use `double` not `float` (portability).** MasoniteORM's `float()` emits `FLOAT(19,4)`, which **Postgres rejects** as a syntax error (broke Test 3 on PG). `double` → `DOUBLE PRECISION` is portable.
3. **`test_i.py` — use builder `update()` instead of instance `save()`** (consistency with `test_j`; avoids instance-level table mis-qualification). Does not change SQLite/PG results; does not resolve the MySQL update bug (that's grammar-level).

## Verification highlights

- **Transactions are real** (Reviewer 596's concern): ran the exact rollback probe on live PG + MySQL — `before 0 / mid 50 / after 0` PASS on both (inserts visible in-txn, gone after rollback). So B/I/J/K measure transactional throughput, not autocommit.
- All recorded numbers are from a single consistent batch (`ITERATIONS=500`).

## Per-DB summary of what's recorded

- **SQLite** — full A–K, Tests 1/2/3.
- **PostgreSQL 17** — full A–K, Tests 1/2/3.
- **MySQL 8** — A–H + Delete (K), Tests 1/2/3. **Update: Whole (I) and Update: Partial (J) = N/A** — upstream MasoniteORM MySQL UPDATE-grammar bug (``SET `users`.<col> … WHERE `users`.id`` → *Unknown column 'users.id'*). MySQL geometric mean is over the available ops.

Upstream `tortoise/orm-benchmarks` PR remains on HOLD.

**Do not merge — for QA + Reviewer 596 delta review.**

items.title: docs: eval Unsloth NVFP4 quants vs nvidia on GB10 — throughput claims invert
items.body:
## Summary
- Add 2026-07-11 evaluation to `llama.cpp/EVALUATIONS.md`: Unsloth "Dynamic NVFP4" Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (+Fast) vs `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`, all on the same vLLM nightly image and serve flags
- Update the `vllm/README.md` model table (94–122 tok/s nightly-dependent, pointer to the new eval)

## Motivation
Unsloth's collection claims 1.56x/1.79x throughput over other NVFP4 quants. Those numbers are 1xB200 @ 128-concurrency; on bandwidth-bound GB10 single-stream the result inverts — nvidia 116–122 tok/s vs Unsloth 99–107 (~15% slower), because Unsloth keeps more layers in FP8 (all attention + lm_head, std also last-8-layers' experts) → 25/23 GB resident vs 22 GB. Recording it keeps the nvidia quant as the default and saves re-testing.

## Notes
- MTP weights intact in all three checkpoints; acceptance marginally higher on Unsloth (0.72 vs 0.69) but doesn't offset the bandwidth cost
- Both Unsloth checkpoints load cleanly on the nightly with the existing `vllm-server.env` flags (compressed-tensors vs modelopt)
- nvidia baseline moved 112 → 122 tok/s since 2026-06-25 (nightly drift) — re-bench baselines when the image is a moving nightly

items.title: spikes: record Spike 2 stress run (100k × 500k, 46.57 GB)
items.body:
## Summary

Records the stress-scale Spike 2 result alongside the small run; updates the spikes README to link both result files with the right framing.

**Headline:** at 50× the prior scale, the load-bearing mmap-share assumption still holds — system RAM delta during the 8-worker mmap-read phase was +0.39 GB against a 372.56 GB worst-case if no sharing. Apparent-to-physical RSS ratio ~520:1.

The script's auto-verdict prints FAIL on parent peak RSS (1051 MB vs 500 MB threshold) and WARN on both throughput numbers. The full results file unpacks why this is over-stated:

- **Parent peak RSS 1051 MB at 46.57 GB file** = 2.1% of file size. Compare to the small run: 184 MB at 1 GB file = 18.4% of file size. The *ratio shrinks* with scale → streaming is working; what grows is allocator high-water mark, not buffer fill. Configurable via memory-pool choice and/or `release_unused()` between batches.
- **Write 157 MB/s, aggregate read 465 MB/s** — host disk is `/tmp` on `/dev/root` (boot disk, not NVMe), and the 46 GB file exceeds the 32 GB host RAM so workers incur cold reads. Plan already calls out NVMe vs HDD as binding at n=1M; this confirms it empirically.

## What this changes

- **5d.1 green light:** unchanged. The architectural bet survives the scale-up.
- **Two follow-ups identified** (recorded in the results file, not yet in the plan):
  1. Sub-spike before 5d.1 build: vary `--batch-size {256, 1024, 4096}` × pool {jemalloc, system}, measure parent peak RSS, pick a known-good default for 5d.1.
  2. Tighten `spike2_arrow_streaming.py`'s verdict thresholds so absolute MB limits become growth-rate-vs-file-size tests — future big runs shouldn't false-fail on monotone allocator high-water mark.

## Test plan

- [x] No code changes; new results file + README link update only.
- [ ] Reviewer sanity-checks the sublinearity claim by comparing parent-peak/file-size ratios across the two runs (18.4% small → 2.1% stress).

items.title: feat(proof): add headless iPhone-to-iPhone proof harness
items.body:
## Summary

Adds `meshlink-proof/scripts/run_headless_ios_ios_proof.py`, the iOS<->iOS
counterpart to the existing Android<->iOS (`run_headless_meshlink_benchmark.py`)
and Android<->Android (`run_android_proof_fleet.py --device ... --device ...`)
proof runners. No harness previously existed for validating two physical
iPhones exchanging directly with each other.

## Design

- Launches one iPhone as a passive receiver (`MESHLINK_DISABLE_AUTO_SEND=true`,
  mirroring the Android passive role in the cross-platform benchmark script)
  and the other as the benchmark sender, both via
  `xcrun devicectl device process launch --console`.
- Gates success on the sender's own scored
  `BENCHMARK transport bytes=... result=Sent` line - the same success gate the
  cross-platform runner uses.
- Requires both `ProofApp.app` copies to already be built/installed (this
  script never invokes `xcodebuild` itself, since there's no single "the"
  device to build for in a two-iPhone scenario). Documented build steps are in
  the README update.

## Validation

Used this script (plus the existing Android<->Android and Android<->iOS
runners) to validate a 2-Android + 2-iOS device matrix - all 6 pairwise
combinations:

| Pair | Result |
|---|---|
| Android1 (Nokia X20) <-> Android2 (A063) | PASS - L2CAP, ack+receipt+identity verified |
| Android1 <-> iOS1 (iPhone 15) | PASS (0.09 KB/s) - 1 transient BLE retry |
| Android2 <-> iOS1 | PASS (0.09 KB/s) - 1 transient BLE retry |
| Android1 <-> iOS2 (iPhone 12 mini) | PASS (0.08 KB/s) |
| Android2 <-> iOS2 | PASS (0.09 KB/s) |
| iOS1 <-> iOS2 | PASS (0.61 / 0.39 KB/s across 2 runs) |

The two transient `ReceiptTimeout` failures were resolved by a clean retry and
are consistent with previously documented BLE flakiness (see
`meshlink-proof/scripts/run_android_proof_fleet.py`'s BLE congestion notes),
not a regression from the recent hop-session replay-protection change (#65).

## Docs

Documents the new script in `meshlink-proof/ios/README.md` (new section 7,
renumbering the trailing section) and `docs/reference/repository-layout.md`.



## Follow-up investigation: why cross-platform runs looked slower, and why retries happened

After merging the original 6-pair validation, investigated two questions: why
Android-involved pairs measured much lower "throughput" than iOS<->iOS, and
why 2 of 4 Android<->iOS pairs needed a retry. This commit adds the
instrumentation that made the real answers possible (BEARER decision/result
logging + `--repeat`) and the findings below come from rerunning the series
with it.

### 1. The 64-byte "throughput" numbers are a measurement artifact, not a bandwidth difference

`throughputKBps = bytes / elapsedMs` at a 64-byte payload measures almost pure
fixed per-message round-trip overhead, not real bandwidth. Confirmed by
rerunning Android1<->iOS1 at 65536 bytes: throughput jumped from ~0.09 KB/s to
33.6 KB/s, both `result=Sent`. Comparing 64-byte "throughput" across platform
pairs is comparing round-trip latency, not data-transfer speed.

### 2. Bearer selection is NOT the cause of the Android<->iOS latency gap (hypothesis refuted)

The leading hypothesis after reading `GattDataBearerModeSupport.kt` and
`docs/explanation/why-l2cap-first.md` was that cross-platform `Data` frames
might still be falling back to the slower GATT path if L2CAP wasn't ready in
time. The new `BEARER decision`/`BEARER result` log lines refute this: across
every rerun of Android1<->iOS1 and Android2<->iOS1 at 64 bytes, `Data` frames
consistently resolved to `mode=L2CAP_PREFERRED_WITH_GATT_FALLBACK
l2capReady=true` and `result=L2CAP` - only the (deliberately GATT_ONLY)
handshake frames used GATT. So the benchmark payload itself is already going
over L2CAP in these pairs; the latency gap has some other cause (most likely
still connection-interval/negotiation differences between cross-vendor
Android-central/iOS-peripheral pairing vs same-vendor iOS<->iOS, but that is
now a separate, narrower question than "which bearer is used").

### 3. The real root cause of the retries: a duplicate `HandshakeMessage2` send races handshake completion (new finding, reproduced 4/5 times)

Rerunning Android2<->iOS1 5x at 64 bytes reproduced the failure far more
reliably than before (4 of 5 runs failed with `ReceiptTimeout`, not 1 of 4).
The `BEARER decision` logging pinpointed the mechanism precisely, identically
in all 4 failures:

1. Android sends `HandshakeMessage2` (`BEARER decision frame=HandshakeMessage2
   mode=GATT_ONLY`).
2. ~1.2-1.3s later, Android sends **a second, independent**
   `HandshakeMessage2` for the same peer (same bearer, GATT_ONLY - this is not
   the dual-bearer race #65's `GattDataBearerModeSupport.kt` fix addressed;
   both sends use the identical single bearer).
3. Shortly after the second send, Android logs
   `DIAG HOP_SESSION_FAILED stage=transport.handshake.message3.process
   reason=DELIVERY_FAILURE cause=AEADBadTagException`.
4. On iOS, the first `HandshakeMessage2` establishes the hop session and route
   normally (`hopSessionEstablished`, `routeDiscovered`), but the *second*
   arrives after that and is logged as
   `hopSessionFailed stage=transport.handshake.message2.unexpected` - a
   duplicate delivery the initiator can't reconcile with its already-completed
   handshake.
5. The overall session is left in an inconsistent state and the benchmark's
   receipt never arrives within the 20s window -> `ReceiptTimeout`.

This is a distinct bug from the implicit-nonce-desync issue fixed in #65 (see
`docs/explanation/hop-session-replay-protection.md`) and from the dual-bearer
handshake race `GattDataBearerModeSupport.kt` already guards against (that fix
prevents the *same* handshake message from riding two bearers at once; this is
Android's handshake-initiation logic apparently re-sending `HandshakeMessage2`
a second time for the same peer while the first attempt is still in flight,
likely a retry/backoff timer firing before the first attempt's `message3`
reply arrives). **Not fixed in this PR** - flagging as a concrete, now
well-evidenced follow-up: the fix likely belongs in whatever schedules the
Android-side handshake-message2 retry (suppress/cancel the retry once message2
has already been sent and a reply is still pending, rather than timer-driven
resend), plus a look at whether `EndToEndSession`'s separate nonce pair (called
out as unaudited in the #65 doc) is implicated when message3 decryption fails
after this race.

### 4. iOS<->iOS at large payloads: reproducible failure, not a harness bug (new finding)

Retested iOS1<->iOS2 at 65536 bytes twice after fixing a real bug in this
harness (the passive device's console-capture thread was only given a 7s
grace period to observe a late-arriving frame before being killed, regardless
of the passive capture's own much larger timeout budget - fixed in this PR).
Even with that fixed, **both retries still failed** with `ReceiptTimeout`
(elapsedMs~21200, throughputKBps~3.0), ruling out the harness as the cause.
Sender and passive logs both show the handshake, route discovery, and the
16-byte warmup message completing successfully - then, within a couple of
seconds, `DIAG routeExpired` / `Peer lost` fires on **both** iPhones, well
before the 65536-byte payload's receipt can complete. This means the
underlying BLE link between the two iPhones is actually dropping during (or
immediately before) the large transfer, not queuing/buffering slowly. Given
iOS<->iOS succeeded reliably at 64 bytes but fails reproducibly at 64KB, this
looks like a genuine transport-stability issue specific to iOS<->iOS under
sustained/longer transfers - not yet root-caused, and not fixed here; logged
as a follow-up needing its own investigation (possibly both iPhones
simultaneously scanning+advertising as peers causing role contention, or a
central/peripheral connection-parameter renegotiation dropping the link mid
transfer).

### Net answers to the original questions

- **"Android is so much slower than iOS"**: mostly a 64-byte throughput-metric
  artifact (round-trip latency, not bandwidth) - confirmed not to be a
  bearer-selection issue via the new logging.
- **"Why 2 retries"**: not generic BLE flakiness as first assumed - it's a
  reproducible (4/5) duplicate-`HandshakeMessage2` race that leaves the hop
  session in a broken state and triggers `AEADBadTagException` on message3.
  This is a real, fixable bug, now precisely diagnosed, tracked as follow-up
  work (not fixed in this PR).

items.title: feat: async connection multiplexing via ConnectionStrategy
items.body:
Addresses outstanding CodeRabbit/Copilot review comments on the async connection-multiplexing PR and fixes the two red CI checks (`check-doc`, `coverage`).

### Error propagation in benches/examples
- `benches/async_strategies.rs`, `benches/resource_usage.rs`: query results and join handles now `.expect(...)` instead of being dropped via `.ok()` / `let _ =`, so failed iterations can no longer inflate throughput/RSS/CPU numbers.
- `examples/multiplexed_async.rs`: the `join_next` loop surfaces `JoinError` instead of silently terminating on the first non-`Ok` task.

### Tests fail fast instead of skipping
- `tests/embedded_integration.rs`: `test_embedded_async_concurrent_single_socket` separates the "no embedded module → skip" probe from client construction, then `.expect(...)`s the build, so a genuine build failure fails the test.

### CI fixes
- `src/client/builder.rs`: removed the broken intra-doc link to `with_connection_strategy` (defined only on the async builder, unresolvable from the generic `impl`), which was failing `check-doc` under `#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links)]`.
- `src/client/builder.rs`: embedded socket setup called `ConnectionAddr::into_connection_info()` without `IntoConnectionInfo` in scope, breaking the `embedded` build (and the `coverage` job). Now uses a fully-qualified trait call:

```rust
let redis_connection_info =
    redis::IntoConnectionInfo::into_connection_info(redis::ConnectionAddr::Unix(
        socket_path.to_path_buf(),
    ))
    .map_err(|err| FalkorDBError::InvalidConnectionInfo(err.to_string()))?;
```

### Docs/lint nits
- `README.md`: bare Redis/FalkorDB URLs converted to markdown links (`rustdoc::bare_urls`).
- `.github/wordlist.txt`: new entries alphabetized to match the existing convention.

labels.name: skip-changeset

items.body:
Pre-HN-launch fix. The README led with `158x faster than styled-components` / `2.8–1034x faster` — but those are isolated `css()`/`styled()` factory microbenchmarks, not render performance. That's the kind of claim a skeptical reader (HN especially) rightly calls out, and it undermines the genuinely strong real-world numbers.

Reframed the Benchmarks section to:
- **Lead with real-world render throughput** (SSR + CSR, the same reproducible numbers as the public writeup): 2.0–3.4× faster than styled-components, 1.3–2.1× than Emotion on SSR.
- **State plainly that CSR mount/update is a statistical tie** — React's reconciler dominates; CSS-in-JS overhead is noise there. (Admitting this earns trust.)
- **Demote microbenchmarks into a `<details>` block** with an explicit 'these are not render performance' caveat.

No number deleted — just honestly contextualized. Bundle claims unchanged (4.82 KB gz, React-externalized, bundlephobia-corroborable).

Docs-only, no code change.

## Summary

- Replace stale mixed-core performance numbers with direct README tables for time, scan throughput, and allocation traffic.
- Record six preselected single-core endpoints against exact upstream and fork revisions.
- Include raw pilot/final samples, environment and command logs, a fixed runner, and a deterministic analyzer.
- Refresh the CI badge and correct stale README statements.

## Results

Across the six primary workloads, the fork reduced time by 30.02% to 98.17%. The README also reports scan MB/s plus `B/op` and `allocs/op`. Allocation traffic is kept separate from retained or peak memory, which this experiment did not measure.

Each endpoint uses 31 paired process executions per revision, alternating arm order on one pinned Graviton3 core. The report uses paired log ratios and Bonferroni-adjusted 99.1667% percentile-bootstrap intervals.

- `go vet -tags purego ./...`

- 31 successful final executions per arm for every primary endpoint

Documentation and benchmark tooling only; no library implementation changes.

This adds a reproducible upstream-versus-fork benchmark workflow and refreshes the README with current results. The fork is reported as 30.02%–98.17% faster across six single-core Graviton3 workloads, with throughput and allocation data; library code is unchanged.

## Why it was needed

The previous performance comparison was stale and difficult to reproduce consistently. This change fixes the benchmark revisions, inputs, environment, sampling protocol, and statistical analysis while correcting related README information.

## How it works

1. `run_upstream_benchmark.sh` validates exact revisions, clean checkouts, and SHA-256 hashes for benchmark inputs.
2. It runs tests and builds identical benchmark binaries under a controlled environment.
3. Benchmarks execute on a configurable pinned CPU with `GOMAXPROCS=1` and alternating upstream/fork order.
4. Pilot and final logs, order files, commands, environment snapshots, and hashes are archived.
5. `analyze_upstream_benchmark.py` parses process blocks, validates sample counts and ordering, then computes paired log-ratio reductions, bootstrap intervals, diagnostics, throughput, and allocation metrics.
6. The README and comparison document publish the resulting tables and caveats.

## Key decisions

- Exact commits and input hashes prevent accidental comparison drift.
- Pairing and alternating execution help control machine-load and order effects.
- Six workloads receive Bonferroni-adjusted 99.1667% bootstrap intervals.
- Allocation traffic is reported separately from retained or peak memory, which was not measured.
- `MatchFirst` is omitted from allocation tables where per-operation allocation comparison is not meaningful.

items.title: feat(core): matrix-absorbed MLA decode over a compressed-latent KV cache

labels.name: area:core
labels.description: mlxcel-core: MLX FFI, primitives, KV cache, layers

items.body:
## Summary

Adds `mlxcel_core::mla`, a shared matrix-absorbed MLA implementation over a compressed-latent KV cache, and wires `deepseek_v2` onto it behind `MLXCEL_MLA_ABSORBED` (default off). Stage 1 (cache format plus absorbed decode from composed MLX ops) and Stage 2 (split-KV reusing issue #898's merge kernel unchanged) both land here; Stage 2's partial producer is composed from MLX ops, not a fused kernel, and is not a speed path.

## A correction to the issue's premise, up front

The issue says the MLA families cache the decompressed K/V. That is true for `deepseek_v2`, `minicpm3`, and `dots1`. It is **not** true for `deepseek_v3` and `deepseek_v32`: both have carried matrix absorption since before this work, decomposing `kv_b_proj` into `embed_q` / `unembed_out` in `sanitize_weights` and caching `(kv_latent, k_pe)` with the rope score passed to SDPA as an additive mask. So the actual gap was V2, MiniCPM3, and dots1, plus the fact that the transform existed twice with no shared home. This PR builds that shared home and moves V2 onto it. V3/V3.2 are untouched (converging them is a follow-up with real regression risk that deserves its own PR), and MiniCPM3/dots1 are untouched and still decompressed.

## What changed

- `src/lib/mlxcel-core/src/mla/absorb.rs`: load-time fold of `kv_b_proj` into `W_UK [1, H, qk_nope, r]` for the query path and `W_UV^T [1, H, r, v_head]` for the output path. Dequantizes when quantized (including the NVFP4 `global_scale` sidecar, folded as a scalar since `(x @ W^T) * s2 == x @ (W * s2)^T`), refuses a biased layer because the identity has no term for a bias, and refuses a geometry that does not partition the matrix. Nothing on disk is touched.
- `src/lib/mlxcel-core/src/mla/cache.rs`: `MlaLatentCache`, a checked view over `KVCache` that puts `ckv` in the key slot and `kpe` in the value slot. `supports()` is split out of `wrap()` so a caller can fall back (the borrow checker keeps the `&mut` alive through the `Err` arm of a `Result` carrying that borrow's lifetime, which would otherwise make the fallback unexpressible). Also the `latent_bytes_per_token` / `decompressed_bytes_per_token` accounting the KV-memory table is computed from.
- `src/lib/mlxcel-core/src/mla/decode.rs`: Stage 1. `SDPA(q_absorbed, ckv, ckv, scale, mask = scale * q_pe @ kpe^T + causal)`. The rope half of the score is additive in exactly SDPA's mask position, so the identity is exact and MLX's fused attention kernel still does the softmax and the value accumulation. Same shape `deepseek_v3.rs` already uses.
- `src/lib/mlxcel-core/src/mla/split_kv.rs`: Stage 2. `MlaSplitPlan` cuts the latent range; each chunk produces a normalized partial and its log2 LSE; `paged_attention_merge_states` merges them.
- `src/lib/mlxcel-core/src/mla/stats.rs`: per-path call counters and a `path=count` summary.
- `src/models/deepseek_v2.rs`: `MLAAttention` gains an optional fold and a `forward_absorbed` branch; `load_mla_attention` builds the fold only under the flag; `report_absorption` prints the load-time decision.
- `examples/mla_absorbed_decode_bench.rs`: three-arm decode benchmark plus the KV-memory table.
- `docs/mla-absorbed-decode.md`, indexed from `docs/README.md`, plus both variables in `docs/environment-variables.md`.

## Why the cache is a view over `KVCache` and not a new type

`LanguageModel::make_caches` returns `Vec<KVCache>` and `forward` takes `&mut [KVCache]`, so a genuinely new cache type forces the family into the `ModelOwnedSequenceState` escape hatch the SSM hybrids use, which costs `supports_batching`, the paged decode backend, and the generic prompt-cache donation path. The FP16 update path already stores keys and values as independent `[B, H, L, D]` buffers reading each side's head dim from its own shape, so a 512-wide "key" beside a 64-wide "value" is already expressible. `offset`, `live_start`, `trim`, `trim_front`, `nbytes`, and `can_trim_prompt_cache` therefore keep their existing meanings on latent rows, and the slot assignment matches what `deepseek_v3.rs` has always done so both describe the same buffer.

## How #898's merge kernel is reused, and whether its contract held

Reused verbatim. No change to `paged_attention_v2_merge.cpp`, to `paged_attention_v2.h`, to the `ffi::paged_attention_merge_states` signature, or to the C++ launcher. MLA fits the documented contract as `H = num_heads`, `D = kv_lora_rank`, `M = batch`, `N = batch * chunks`, and `o_indptr` request-major. The contract held unchanged; the only thing the new caller had to honour rather than discover is the **log2 LSE** clause, which is the one that fails silently: a natural-log LSE still merges and returns a plausible wrong weighted average. It is a named constant (`split_kv::LOG2_E`) with a comment, and `merge_rejects_natural_log_lse_units` is a negative control that asserts the natural-log variant does *not* match a host f64 reference while the log2 variant does. `split_kv_matches_the_decompressed_reference_at_every_chunk_length` restates, at the MLA caller, the regrouping property `paged_v2::launch_tests::merge_is_associative_across_regroupings` pins for the kernel.

## Verified vs unverified

**Verified, on synthetic tensors with MLA geometry against a host-side f64 reference that performs the pre-absorption computation:** the absorption identity in f32 and f16; that the additive causal mask survives being merged into the rope score (with a positive control asserting the mask actually changes the answer, so the masked test cannot pass on a no-op); the up-projection direction of the fold; the `(ckv, kpe)` packing round-tripping through a real `KVCache` including the append boundary; that a latent cache stays trimmable so speculative decode's reject path removes one latent row per token; the split-and-merge decomposition at four chunk lengths and against the unsplit Stage 1 answer; the log2 LSE negative control; and, through `deepseek_v2`'s own `MLAAttention::forward`, that a 6-token prefill plus 4 decode steps produce the same block output (through `o_proj`) with and without the fold, step for step, and that the resulting cache is more than 3x smaller.

**Not verified:** anything against a real MLA checkpoint. No DeepSeek-family checkpoint is available on this host (the locally available models are Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3-0.6B, and gemma-3-1b, none of them MLA, and a DeepSeek-V3-class checkpoint does not fit in 128 GB). So the issue's token-parity gate on pinned DeepSeek oracles is **not** satisfied by this PR, and the flag stays default-off for exactly that reason. Nothing here should be read as real-model validation.

**No benchmarks were run.** The harness is written and smoke-tested for correctness on a toy geometry only; all throughput numbers are for the reviewer to produce.

## CUDA

No CUDA was written in this PR, so there is no new unvalidated CUDA to declare. Stage 2 reuses #898's merge kernel, which already ships a structurally parallel CUDA port that #898 declared unvalidated; that status is unchanged. The issue asked for a fused MLA partial kernel with CUDA first, and that is deliberately not in this PR: a fused partial kernel is the thing that would make Stage 2 faster, and it should be written after Stage 1's measurements justify it (as the issue itself scopes it) and against a host that can validate at least one of the two backends. The interactions the issue lists are unaffected: `kv_a_layernorm` is untouched, so the CUDA RMSNorm overlay (#829) sits where it sat; nothing here assumes CUDA graph replay.

## How to run the benchmark, and how to prove which path it took

```
export DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode-26.6.0.app/Contents/Developer
cargo run --release --features metal,accelerate --example mla_absorbed_decode_bench -- \
    --contexts 4096,16384,32768 --batches 1,4 --steps 64 --warmup 16
```

Three arms per (context, batch): `decompressed`, `absorbed`, `split_kv`. Every row ends in a `paths=` field read from `mlxcel_core::mla::stats`, taken and reset around the measured region, and the harness prints a `WARNING` on any row whose counters disagree with its arm's label. A correct run looks like `decompressed=64 absorbed_prefill=0 absorbed_composed=0 absorbed_split_kv=0` on the first arm and `... absorbed_composed=64 ...` on the second; an "absorbed" row reading `absorbed_composed=0` is measuring the fallback and must not be reported. `split_kv` is expected to be slower than `absorbed` here, because its partials are composed from MLX ops rather than fused; that arm exists to show the decomposition running, not to be quoted.

For a real checkpoint, `MLXCEL_MLA_ABSORBED=1 mlxcel generate -m models/<deepseek> ...` prints one stdout line at load stating how many layers folded and the bytes/token before and after. A run whose line reads `0/N layers` is running the fallback. Both signals go to stdout rather than through `tracing` because the `mlxcel` CLI installs no tracing subscriber, so `tracing::info!` on this path emits nothing at any `RUST_LOG`.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test --release -p mlxcel-core --lib --features metal,accelerate mla::` — 33 passed, 0 failed
- [x] `cargo test --release -p mlxcel-core --lib --features metal,accelerate paged_v2::` — 55 passed, 0 failed (the reused merge kernel and its regrouping property)
- [x] `cargo test --release --lib --features metal,accelerate models::deepseek` — 32 passed, 0 failed (V2 wiring parity plus the untouched V3 / V3.2 suites)
- [x] `cargo clippy -p mlxcel-core --lib --tests --features metal,accelerate -- -D warnings` — clean
- [x] `cargo clippy --lib --tests --example mla_absorbed_decode_bench --features metal,accelerate -- -D warnings` — clean
- [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- [x] `python3 scripts/ci/check_cross_repo_refs.py` — exit 0
- [x] Benchmark harness smoke-run on a toy geometry: all three arms execute and each reports its own path

The full `cargo test -p mlxcel-core` sweep was not run: it exceeds this environment's watchdog. Its known pre-existing failure on this base commit is `fused_moe_parity_tests::fused_moe_geglu_kernel_matches_references_gemma4_shape` (tracked as #964), untouched here.

## Left out, deliberately

Fused Stage 2 partial kernel (Metal and CUDA). MiniCPM3 and dots1 wiring. Converging `deepseek_v3` / `deepseek_v32` onto the shared module. Absorbed prefill (prefill up-projects through the still-loaded `kv_b_proj`, which keeps prefill arithmetic identical to the baseline but makes a chunked prefill re-up-project rows it already handled). Paged-backed and non-FP16 latent caches, both declined with a message. Any default-on change: the flag stays off until real-checkpoint token parity exists.

Closes #907

items.title: v0.6.0: coalesced partition histogram, benchmark timing fix, and correctness fixes
items.body:
## Summary

- fix: `bench/vulkan_benchmark.cc` measured real Vulkan GPU time only when `--timestamps` was passed; otherwise it silently aliased CPU time, so every default-mode Vulkan benchmark row reported identical GPU/CPU numbers. Add a lightweight always-on 2-timestamp query pool (matching `fuchsia_benchmark.cc`) so GPU total time is always accurate. Also switch the key-value benchmark sort from indirect (GPU-buffer element count) to direct, dropping an extra buffer/copy per call.
- perf: transpose `partitionHistogram`'s layout so upsweep's write is partition-major (coalesced for upsweep) while spine's write stays radix-major (coalesced for spine) — previously one of the two was always strided. Net result: keys-only throughput now edges out Fuchsia radix sort instead of trailing it.
- fix: `upsweep`/`downsweep` now return early once `partitionStart >= elementCount`, skipping wasted work for padding partitions that only arise on indirect sorts (upper-bound `elementCount` larger than the runtime count). The check is workgroup-uniform and placed before any barrier, so it's safe.
- fix: `spine`'s partition-scan loop had a per-thread-dependent trip count whenever `partitionCount` wasn't a multiple of `WORKGROUP_SIZE`, and the loop body contains barriers — barriers require uniform participation across the whole workgroup. Loop bound is now uniform; the per-iteration load/store is guarded separately.
- docs: refresh README benchmark numbers and table (now shows GPU/CPU throughput per backend), note subgroup-size 32 tuning (64 works but may be slower; 16-or-fewer unsupported), and update `media/results.png`.
- bump version to 0.6.0, with `include/vk_radix_sort.h` regenerated to match.

## Test plan

- [x] Rebuild and run `./build/bench vulkan` / `cuda` / `fuchsia` sweeps; confirm GPU and CPU times now differ appropriately in default mode
- [x] Run correctness checks (keys-only and key-value) across a range of N, including sizes that aren't a multiple of `PARTITION_SIZE` or `WORKGROUP_SIZE`

items.title: Add FastAPI-Startkit ORM benchmark (A–K, Tests 1–3)
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a complete benchmark for the **FastAPI-Startkit ORM** (async-adapted MasoniteORM on SQLAlchemy's async engine) — all 11 operations (**A–K**) across all three model shapes (**Test 1** simple, **Test 2** FK relations, **Test 3** wide 32+ field model), matching the other ORMs in the suite.

Self-contained single commit off the suite baseline, so it can also serve as the upstream contribution to `tortoise/orm-benchmarks`.

## Approach

- **Public API only.** Boots the framework as a headless **console app** — `Application(providers=[(DatabaseProvider, DatabaseConfig)])`, no `FastAPIProvider`, no web server. Uses only `fastapi_startkit.masoniteorm` (`Model`, `DatabaseProvider`, `SQLiteConfig`/`MySQLConfig`/`PostgresConfig`, `DB`). No private internals, no `PYTHONPATH` hacks.
- **models.py** — `TEST` selects the model shape; a `row()` helper merges wide-model defaults into inserts; the schema builder creates matching tables (FK column + `journal_related` join table for Test 2, 32+ typed columns for Test 3).
- **test_a … test_k** — insert single/batch/bulk, filter large/small/dict/tuple, get, update whole/partial, delete. Semantics mirror `benchmarks/django`.
- Wired into `benchmarks/bench.sh` (Tests 1–3), `pyproject.toml` (`fastapi-startkit[database,sqlite,postgres,mysql]>=0.46.0`), and the README ORM table.

## Design note — sequential by necessity

The other async ORMs run each op under `asyncio.gather` with `CONCURRENTS` independent sessions. MasoniteORM routes through a **single shared connection manager**, which SQLAlchemy's async engine cannot use safely from concurrent tasks (it raises `transaction already deassociated from connection`). So these tests run **sequentially**. On SQLite this is irrelevant (writes serialize on one connection anyway); on Postgres/MySQL the numbers reflect single-connection throughput. Documented in the benchmark README.

## Verification (SQLite, all green)

All 11 ops run for TEST=1/2/3. Sample (ITERATIONS=500, rows/sec):

items.title: feat(benchmark): reproducible LocalStack Lambda benchmark suite
items.body:
Closes #45.

Adds a reproducible benchmark that gives the before/after comparison requested in #45: **serverless-mysql** vs the naive **mysql2 connection-per-call** model, using a *real Lambda fleet* (LocalStack) against a connection-constrained MySQL.

## What it measures

For each concurrency level, a fixed-duration concurrent workload hits each driver while the DB's open-connection count is sampled. Reports success rate (+ failure codes), peak connections, throughput, and p50/p95/p99 latency.

## Committed results

<!-- numbers refreshed automatically on every release -->

| Driver | Concurrency | Success rate | Throughput (inv/s) | Peak conns | Failures |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| serverless-mysql (managed) | 20 | 100% | 170.5 | 21 | — |
| raw mysql2 (per-call) | 20 | 98.7% | 155.8 | 31 | ER_CON_COUNT_ERROR×17 |
| serverless-mysql (managed) | 30 | 100% | 157.3 | 27 | — |
| raw mysql2 (per-call) | 30 | 97.4% | 129.2 | 31 | ER_CON_COUNT_ERROR×29 |

serverless-mysql holds **100% success** while keeping peak connections **under** the `max_connections=30` cap; raw mysql2 saturates the cap and starts failing with `ER_CON_COUNT_ERROR` once concurrency reaches it.

## Contents

- `benchmark/` — docker-compose stack, Lambda handler (`managed`/`raw` drivers), build + driver (deploys via the AWS SDK, runs the workload, polls connections, writes `results.json`/`results.md`).
- `update-readme.js` injects the table into the README between `<!-- BENCHMARK:START/END -->` markers.
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` refreshes the README benchmark section automatically on every tagged release (`v*`).
- npm scripts: `benchmark`, `benchmark:readme`.

## Honest caveats

Run on a single host via LocalStack, which *emulates* Lambda — container reuse/concurrency and cold-start timing differ from real AWS, and Community-edition concurrency is throttled (default levels capped at 30; higher levels can wedge LocalStack). Numbers illustrate the connection-management **mechanism and relative behavior**, not absolute production SLAs. See `benchmark/README.md` for full methodology.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run lint` passes (benchmark dir is eslint-ignored like `test`/`scripts`)
- [x] `npm run test:unit` passes
- [x] Full benchmark run completes cleanly and produces the committed `results.*`

items.title: feat: search outbox indexing latency 관측 추가
items.body:
## Summary
- Add persisted SQL measurement for search outbox total indexing lag and queue/status counts.
- Add minimal relay timing logs for decomposed latency without changing schema or relay behavior.
- Document how to combine SQL output with `product_search_outbox_indexing_latency` logs for a local synthetic single-document baseline.

## Changed files
- `db/experiments/a1-search-outbox-indexing-latency/README.md`
- `db/experiments/a1-search-outbox-indexing-latency/observations.md`
- `db/experiments/a1-search-outbox-indexing-latency/sql/measure-indexing-lag.sql`
- `src/main/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/domain/SearchOutboxEvent.java`
- `src/main/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/repository/SearchOutboxClaimDao.java`
- `src/main/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/service/ProductSearchOutboxRelayService.java`
- `src/test/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/repository/SearchOutboxClaimDaoTest.java`
- `src/test/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/repository/SearchOutboxStoreTest.java`
- `src/test/java/com/portfolio/marketplace/productsearch/service/ProductSearchOutboxRelayServiceTest.java`

## What indexing latency means
Indexing latency is the time from a product change event being captured in `search_outbox` until the relay finishes the corresponding OpenSearch write/delete and records the final outbox state.

Persisted total lag is defined as:

```text
total_indexing_lag_ms = processed_at - created_at
```

## Why total lag alone is insufficient
`processed_at - created_at` combines queue wait and relay work into one number. It does not show whether delay came from waiting in `search_outbox`, loading the source document from DB, writing to OpenSearch, or updating the outbox row state.

## Metrics added
SQL metrics:
- `total_indexing_lag_ms` p50 / p95 / p99 / max for `DONE` rows
- `pending_count`
- `processing_count`
- `failed_count`
- `done_count`
- `oldest_pending_age_ms`
- retry count distribution

Relay timing log fields:
- `queueWaitMs`
- `sourceDocumentLoadMs`
- `openSearchWriteMs`
- `outboxStateTransitionMs`
- `relayProcessingMs`

## How decomposed latency is measured
The DB schema is unchanged. `SearchOutboxClaimDao` returns existing `created_at` plus `updated_at AS claimed_at` after the claim update. The relay uses those values to calculate `queueWaitMs` and uses local monotonic timing around source load, OpenSearch write/delete, and outbox state transition calls.

The relay emits structured log lines like:

```text
product_search_outbox_indexing_latency eventId=... aggregateId=... eventType=... resultStatus=... queueWaitMs=... sourceDocumentLoadMs=... openSearchWriteMs=... outboxStateTransitionMs=... relayProcessingMs=...
```

No new persistent timing columns are added, and missing persisted timestamps are not fabricated.

## Commands run
- `.\gradlew.bat test`

## Test results
- Full test suite: pass

## Measured local results
No controlled local smoke measurement was executed for this PR.

This PR adds measurement infrastructure only. No latency numbers, throughput numbers, RPS numbers, or benchmark results are recorded.

## Explicit exclusions
- No Bulk Indexing
- No batch size tuning
- No k6 benchmark
- No circuit breaker change
- No OpenSearch mapping change
- No fallback behavior change
- No claim behavior change
- No retry/backoff change
- No scheduler delay change
- No production SLO/SLA claim
- No invented performance numbers

## Remaining limitations
- Persisted SQL can derive total lag and queue/status counts only from existing `search_outbox` columns.
- Step-level breakdown is emitted as relay runtime logs, not stored in the database.
- No local smoke artifact was produced in this PR.
- The next measured result must be labeled local synthetic/local smoke, not production capacity or SLO/SLA.

## Recommended next step
- Run a controlled local single-document relay smoke, capture `product_search_outbox_indexing_latency` logs, and run `measure-indexing-lag.sql` against the same window or `smokeRun` marker to establish the single-document indexing latency baseline.

items.title: Implement thread-per-call GVL release to unblock async reactor Fibers (#64)
items.body:
## Summary

Closes #38, Closes #64.

Stacked on this branch's own hill commits (originally the failing-test PR for
issue #38) — implements the fix and merges it in.

- Splits the native entrypoint out to `Duckling::Native.parse` (no thread spawn, no GVL-release considerations at the call site). `Duckling.parse` (`lib/duckling.rb`) is a thin Ruby-level wrapper that dispatches through `Thread.new { Native.parse(...) }.value` **only when a `Fiber.scheduler` is installed on the calling thread** — a plain thread pool (Puma/Sidekiq-style, no reactor to yield to) already gets its concurrency from `Native.parse`'s own GVL release, so it skips the thread spawn entirely and calls `Native.parse` directly.
- `Duckling::Native.parse` releases the GVL around `duckling::parse` via the raw `rb_thread_call_without_gvl` FFI (Magnus 0.8.2 has no safe wrapper for this). Only plain owned Rust data (`ParsePayload`, stack-local, no heap allocation) crosses the off-GVL boundary — no `magnus::Value`/`magnus::Error` in either direction, per this repo's established GC-safety rule.
- The off-GVL callback wraps the call in `std::panic::catch_unwind` unconditionally, since the wrapped `duckling` crate's own panic guard is compiled out under `debug_assertions` (this repo's own `dev`-profile local default). A caught panic surfaces to the caller as a rescuable `RuntimeError` with the original message preserved (not magnus's own `Error::from_panic` convention of the unrescuable `fatal`).
- A bare GVL release alone is *not* sufficient to unblock an `Async::Reactor` (confirmed by the empirical spike on [the wiki](https://github.com/cpb/duckling/wiki/research-fiber-scheduler-mechanism-spike) — Ruby 3.4's `Fiber::Scheduler#blocking_operation_wait` needs a flag `rb_thread_call_without_gvl` never sets) — the `Thread.new` piece is what actually lets the calling Fiber yield via `Thread#value`'s scheduler hooks. The spawned thread also disables `report_on_exception` from its first line, so a rescued error doesn't also print a thread-termination backtrace to stderr.
- Extends the benchmark suite with a dispatch-mode dimension: `Duckling::Native.parse` (no thread) vs `Duckling.parse` (thread-per-call, measured under an active Fiber scheduler via a `Sync` block — see "Benchmark data" below for why that matters), with a grouped-bar chart and per-scenario overhead percentage in the generated `docs/benchmarks/README.md`. Gracefully omitted for older recorded entries that predate this schema.
- Updated `AGENTS.md`'s `lib/duckling.rb` directory-layout entry and "Rust/Magnus wiring" section to document the `Fiber.scheduler` gating, the rescuable-panic behavior, and (per review) that this gem's `require_relative`-based loading has no interaction with a consuming app's Zeitwerk setup. Added a "Code comment conventions" section documenting that comments should explain durable rationale, not narrate which issue/PR added them.
- Dropped `test/duckling_test.rb`'s hardcoded `Duckling::VERSION` equality test (per review) — needed a manual bump every release with no regression-catching value.

### Additional hardening from review

An earlier review round (findings posted inline, most-severe first) caught:
- Unconditional thread-per-call taxing every synchronous caller — fixed via the `Fiber.scheduler` gating above.
- The stderr backtrace noise on rescued errors — fixed via `report_on_exception = false`.
- The unrescuable `fatal` panic class — fixed via a rescuable `RuntimeError`.
- Along the way, found and fixed a real bug independent of the above: `panic_message`'s downcast took `&panic_payload` where `panic_payload: Box<dyn Any + Send>` — since `Box<dyn Any + Send>` itself implements `Any`, that reference coerced to treat the *Box* as the payload rather than dereferencing into it, so the downcast always missed and every panic message was silently discarded. Fixed to `&*panic_payload`.

## Benchmark data

Also found and fixed a bug in `run_ips`'s own dispatch-mode measurement:
`x.report(name) { ... }` inside `Benchmark.ips do |x| ... end` only
*registers* a block — the timed execution (`job.run`) happens after that
surrounding block returns. Wrapping just the registration loop in `Sync do
... end` therefore measured nothing (by execution time, `Fiber.scheduler`
was already back to `nil`), producing backwards results (dispatch reading
as *faster* than native on some scenarios). Fixed by wrapping the entire
`Benchmark.ips` call — registration and `job.run` — in one `Sync` block, so
the dispatch scenarios actually take the thread-spawn path they're meant to
measure. Re-verified: `empty` (the fastest, most overhead-sensitive
scenario) now reads ~11x slower dispatched vs native, consistent in
direction and rough magnitude with `github-actions`/`claude-code-web`'s
existing recorded data; `long`/`camping_trip_email` show negligible
overhead, as expected.

Re-recorded `docs/benchmarks/local/0.2.1-rc1.json` with the fixed
methodology and the `Fiber.scheduler`-gating code change together.

**Known-stale data, not fixed in this PR:** `docs/benchmarks/github-actions/0.2.1-rc1.json`
and `docs/benchmarks/claude-code-web/0.2.1-rc1.json` were recorded *before*
the `Fiber.scheduler`-gating fix landed, when `Duckling.parse` unconditionally
spawned a Thread on every call. Their dispatch-overhead (ips vs native_ips)
numbers are still directionally valid (that code path always paid the
thread-spawn tax back then, same effect as today's `Sync`-wrapped
measurement) — but their **concurrency/throughput** numbers are now stale:
`efficiency_pct` reads 20.4% (github-actions) / 23.7% (claude-code-web) vs
local's fresh 62.6%, purely because the plain-thread-pool concurrency
benchmark no longer pays a per-call thread-spawn tax after the gating fix,
and only `local`'s data reflects that yet. In the generated README this
currently reads as an environment/hardware difference when it's actually a
code-version difference within the data itself.
- `github-actions` can't be refreshed pre-merge: `benchmark-branch.yml`
  (this PR's own generalized, `workflow_dispatch`-only replacement for the
  old push-triggered scaffolding) isn't dispatchable against this branch
  until it exists on `main` — confirmed via `gh workflow run` (404). Refresh
  via `gh workflow run benchmark-branch.yml --ref main` (or the normal
  `benchmark.yml` dispatch) once merged.
- `claude-code-web` can only be recorded from an actual Claude Code Web
  remote session (`CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE=true`) — needs a follow-up
  `bundle exec rake benchmark:record_pr` run from such a session.

## Test plan
- [x] `test/falcon_fiber_blocking_test.rb` (the failing test this hill introduced) now passes
- [x] `test/thread_pool_dispatch_test.rb` — plain thread-pool callers (no `Fiber.scheduler`) spawn zero per-call `Thread`s
- [x] `test/parse_error_stderr_test.rb` — rescued errors write nothing to stderr
- [x] `test/native_panic_test.rb` — a native panic surfaces as a rescuable `StandardError` with its message preserved, and the process survives
- [x] `bundle exec rake` (standard + compile + test) green
- [x] `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` clean
- [x] Ran the real `bundle exec rake benchmark:record` (not just fixture-based unit tests) to confirm the corrected dispatch-mode ips comparison actually executes, produces sane (non-backwards) numbers, and is recorded to `docs/benchmarks/local/`
- [x] New unit tests for `DucklingBenchmark::Report.build_dispatch_section`, including a legacy-entry-without-native-data case (backward compat)

```
Expected every ticker Fiber tick inside the Async::Reactor to stay within 0.011s of the
requested 0.001s interval (i.e. Duckling.parse does NOT stall sibling Fibers), but the
largest observed gap was 0.173s, while the measured Duckling.parse call itself took
0.1726s. A max gap approximately equal to the parse duration is exactly the signature
predicted by the blocking-FFI-call risk claim: Duckling.parse holds the GVL for its
entire native execution and never yields to the async reactor, so the ticker Fiber (and
every other Fiber on this reactor thread) is frozen for the duration of the parse call.
Expected 0.17297000001417473 to be < 0.011.
```

This is a real, empirically measured result (reproduced multiple times locally, gap ≈
parse duration each run), not a placeholder — the test's assertion encodes the
*non-blocking* null hypothesis on purpose, so a failure here is itself the empirical
confirmation of the Falcon Fiber-blocking claim in the
[`research-ffi-risks`](https://github.com/cpb/duckling/wiki/research-ffi-risks) wiki
page's risk analysis.

## Notes for the implementation session

- The test currently emits `Async::Task#sleep is deprecated, use Kernel#sleep instead`
  warnings from the installed `async` gem version — cosmetic, does not affect the result,
  but worth a quick look during implementation.

## Reviewer instructions

Review the expected failure message above. If it correctly specifies the intended
behavior per the issue, **remove the `hill-ready` label** from this PR — that signals
the implementation session to begin. Run `/continue-pr 38` (this PR) to start it.

</details>

items.title: Separate test suite taxonomy
items.body:
﻿## Summary

Closes #55.

This PR separates OmniKV's test evidence into clearer categories so CI and docs no longer blur debug, demonstration, regression, release-gate, and performance-smoke suites.

## What changed

- Renamed the old debug integration tests into explicit regression suites:
  - `compaction_regression`
  - `compaction_many_records_regression`
  - `reopen_regression`
- Replaced print-only debug checks with assertions that prove:
  - manual compaction preserves a committed key;
  - many-record compaction preserves first, middle, and last records;
  - reopen after compaction preserves values and sequence progress.
- Updated CI job names so suites are easier to read as evidence:
  - compaction/reopen regression tests;
  - storage performance smoke;
  - SSI anomaly demonstration tests.
- Added `docs/test-suite-taxonomy.md` explaining release gates, regression suites, demos, perf smoke, and manual/long-running evidence.
- Linked the taxonomy from `README.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test compaction_regression -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test compaction_many_records_regression -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test reopen_regression -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test anomaly_demos -- --test-threads=1`
- `cargo clippy -p omnikv-engine --all-targets -j 2 -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test storage_perf -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p omnikv-engine --test benchmarks --release -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture`

## Notes

The benchmark smoke suite records throughput output, but this PR intentionally treats those numbers as informational. CI should gate semantic equivalence and basic performance regressions, not make formal benchmark claims from variable hosted runners.

items.title: feat(throughput): make cumulative tok/s the headline metric
items.body:
## Summary

Decode-only throughput hides prefill-engine gains that are a real,
consumer-visible latency win: two models with identical decode speed but a
4-6x prefill gap are not equivalent in practice, yet a decode-only headline
number reports them as if they were. The correct consumer-facing measure is
cumulative: `(prompt_tokens + completion_tokens) / total_wall_clock_seconds`.

- Promotes the ad hoc throughput probe (previously an untracked personal
  script) to a tracked harness, `harness/throughput/run.py`, adding a
  `cumulative_tok_s` field per run plus median/min/max in its summary block —
  first-listed (headline), ahead of the existing `decode_tok_s`/`prefill_tok_s`.
- `schema.json`'s `total_tokens_per_second` field was already defined as
  exactly this cumulative formula — no new field is added; instead its
  description (and `decode_tokens_per_second`'s) is updated to make the
  headline/supporting-detail split explicit. Purely additive: no field
  added, removed, or renamed, so older published rows stay fully valid.
- `docs/schema.md`, `README.md`, and `RANKINGS.md` explain the rationale.
  `RANKINGS.md`'s numeric leaderboard cells are left untouched — this PR is a
  metric-*definition* change, not a data recompute; historical rows are
  flagged as legacy pending the next publish cycle.
- Two small doc comments in `vllm.py`/`bench_serve.py` tie their existing
  (unchanged) `throughput_total_toks_per_s` / `throughput_output_toks_per_s`
  metric rows to the new headline policy.

Not in scope (explicitly): no HuggingFace publish, no new `mlx-bench-publish`
converter kind for the harness's raw JSON shape (it was never wired to
publish before this PR) — wiring it up is a reasonable follow-up but wasn't
requested and would be its own PR.

items.title: MiniOneRec parity, DDP training path, and per-step performance optimizations
items.body:
## Summary

This PR adds a full **MiniOneRec** recipe to verl-GR (dataset, constrained beam rollout, rule + NDCG rewards, `minionerec_reinforce` loss) and closes much of the **~2× per-step gap** vs upstream MiniOneRec (`~2.2s` → verl was `~4.1–4.5s` before optimizations). It also merges **RankGRPO** work from `main`, resolves conflicts, and documents the behavioral mapping vs `MiniOneRec/rl.sh`.

Primary training entry: `scripts/run_minionerec_grpo_rl_aligned.sh` (4-GPU, hyperparameters aligned with `MiniOneRec/rl.sh`).

---

## What changed

### MiniOneRec recipe (new vs `main`)

| Area | Key files | Notes |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Data | `minionerec_dataset.py`, `minionerec_format.py` | `SidDataset`-style prompts; `RLTitle2Sid` / `RLSeqTitle2Sid` with `seq_title_sample=10000` |
| Rollout | `constrained_beam_agent_loop.py`, `hf_constrained_generation.py`, `minionerec_fsdp_workers.py` | **HF constrained beam** on DDP (parity with original `generate`); prefix-trie from `info_file` |
| Reward | `minionerec_reward.py` | Rule + group NDCG ranking; training penalties for empty / invalid SID |
| Loss | `minionerec_loss.py` | `minionerec_reinforce` — skips redundant `old_log_prob` forward when configured |
| Trainer | `minionerec_trainer.py`, `minionerec_recipe.py` | Validation HR/NDCG, reward postprocess, engine optimizations |

Docs: `docs/verl_gr/minionerec_mapping.md`, `docs/verl_gr/minionerec_pr_changes.md`.

### DDP training path

- Configs: `configs/verl_gr/minionerec/grpo_trainer_ddp.yaml`, `minionerec_ddp_actor.yaml`, `minionerec_ddp_ref.yaml`
- Engine: `verl_gr/workers/engine/ddp/transformer_impl.py` — PyTorch DDP LM-head engine (lighter than FSDP for this workload)
- Launcher mapping (`run_minionerec_grpo_rl_aligned.sh` ↔ `MiniOneRec/rl.sh`):

| `rl.sh` | verl-GR |
|---------|---------|
| 4 processes | `N_GPUS=4` |
| `train_batch_size=64` completions | `TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE=32` prompts × `BEAM_WIDTH=16` = **512 completions/step** |
| `gradient_accumulation_steps=2` | `PPO_MICRO_BATCH_PER_GPU=2` |
| `num_train_epochs=2` | `TOTAL_EPOCHS=2` |
| `num_generations=16` | `BEAM_WIDTH=16` |
| `learning_rate=1e-5` | `LEARNING_RATE=1e-5` |
| `beta=1e-3` | `kl_loss_coef=0.001` |
| `test_during_training=False` | `trainer.val_before_train=false` |

### Performance optimizations

1. **`completion_only_logprob` (`logits_to_keep`)** — `verl_gr/workers/engine/completion_only_logprob.py`, `minionerec_engine_patch.py`  
   - Ref (`forward_only`): padded forward + `logits_to_keep` (closer to TRL `_get_per_token_logps`)  
   - Actor (train): rmpad forward + completion-only logprob gather  
   - Cuts heavy ref/update work vs full-sequence vocab softmax

2. **`paged_adamw_32bit`** — `verl_gr/workers/optimizer.py` (requires `bitsandbytes`; matches MiniOneRec low-LR stability)

3. **Trainer shortcuts** — `RLTrainer`: skip `old_log_prob` forward when `loss_mode=minionerec_reinforce`; rmpad + chunked entropy to avoid OOM

4. **NVTX profiling (optional)** — ranges: `gen.generate`, `ref.forward`, `reward.compute`, `actor.forward_backward`, `logprob.completion_only`; compare with `scripts/compare_nsys_nvtx.py` (~10–40% step overhead when profiling is on)

### RankGRPO merge

- Resolves merge conflicts with `main` / RankGRPO (#35)
- Restores `rankgrpo_algorithm.py` helpers and `beam_backend.py` fix for `stochastic_constrained` (sampled token, not top-logprob)
- `_prune_unkept_checkpoint_dirs` in `rl_trainer.py` for rankgrpo tests

### Scripts & hygiene

**Kept:** `run_minionerec_grpo_rl_aligned.sh` (primary), `run_minionerec_grpo.sh`, `compare_nsys_nvtx.py`  
**Removed:** ablation helpers (`run_ablation_*`, `analyze_ablation_training.py`, `run_minionerec_grpo_stabilized.sh`)  
**Renamed tests:** `test_minionerec_completion_only_logprob.py`, `test_minionerec_reward_penalties.py`  
**`.gitignore`:** `nsys/`, `*.nsys-rep`, `profiles/`

All launcher comments are now **English**.

---

## Why

- verl-GR’s generic RL loop treated **ref logprob** and **actor update** as separate full forward passes over padded sequences, roughly doubling LM-head cost vs MiniOneRec’s TRL path.
- MiniOneRec needs **constrained beam** and **completion-only logprobs**; this PR implements those in the recipe/engine layer rather than only in the trainer.
- RankGRPO on `main` had to be integrated without regressing MiniOneRec or rankgrpo unit tests.

---

## How to test

```bash
cd verl-GR

# Unit / contract tests
PYTHONPATH="${PWD}:${PWD}/../verl" python tests/test_minionerec_parity.py
PYTHONPATH="${PWD}:${PWD}/../verl" python tests/test_minionerec_completion_only_logprob.py
PYTHONPATH="${PWD}:${PWD}/../verl" python tests/test_minionerec_reward_penalties.py
PYTHONPATH="${PWD}:${PWD}/../verl" python -m pytest tests/test_rankgrpo_loss_modes.py -q

# Smoke train (set BASE_MODEL and data paths; train_max_samples >= TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE)
export BASE_MODEL=/path/to/checkpoint
export MINIONEREC_ROOT=/path/to/MiniOneRec
bash scripts/run_minionerec_grpo_rl_aligned.sh \
  ++data.train_max_samples=64 ++data.val_max_samples=0

# Optional Nsight (requires nsys in PATH)
# Wrap the same command with nsys profile ... and compare:
# python scripts/compare_nsys_nvtx.py baseline_nvtxsum.csv optimized_nvtxsum.csv
```

**Checklist**

- [ ] `test_minionerec_*` and `test_rankgrpo_loss_modes` pass locally  
- [ ] 4-GPU aligned run reaches steady steps without OOM (`use_remove_padding`, chunked entropy enabled)  
- [ ] Per-step time closer to MiniOneRec baseline (ref + update no longer dominate)  
- [ ] WandB / offline logging as expected  

---

## Known limitations

- **DDP training uses HF constrained beam**, not vLLM async beam — async/vLLM remains a separate path (OpenOneRec two-stage beam lives under rollout server / engine).
- **Semantic / SASRec rewards** not ported (rule + ranking only).
- **Full multi-epoch parity** vs upstream MiniOneRec still needs cluster runs; CI is unit/contract level.
- **`train_max_samples` must be ≥ `TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE`** or the dataloader is empty.
- **vLLM + `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments`** are incompatible (documented in `run_minionerec_grpo_rl_aligned.sh`).
- **Nsight** adds measurable overhead; use only for profiling, not for final throughput numbers.

---

## Related docs

- `docs/verl_gr/minionerec_mapping.md` — behavioral contract vs MiniOneRec  
- `docs/verl_gr/minionerec_pr_changes.md` — reviewer-oriented change list  
- `scripts/README.md` — launcher index  

---

items.title: Opus 5 alignment: deferred follow-ups
items.body:
Follow-up to #3 (merged). Clears the four items that PR deliberately deferred — nothing here is broken today; the theme is instructions written for an older model that now push Opus 5 the wrong way.

## Closes the residual #3 admitted to

#3 relaxed the rules layer while `cook/SKILL.md` still said **"Always spawn"** for testing and review, and declared a workflow ending with zero `Task` calls to be a contract violation. So `/ck:cook` kept forcing subagents on small work regardless of the gate.

The contract is now about the *outcome*: testing, review, and finalization must all happen. Whether each spawns a subagent is the gate's call — skipping one is still a violation, doing it inline below the gate is not.

`references/workflow-steps.md:276` carried the same zero-Task-calls rule. The plan flagged that a relaxed table beside a still-mandatory reference file is worse than either alone, so a grep found it and both moved together.

## Triggers that no longer set anything

`bootstrap` had a **Thinking** column in its mode table and a `**Thinking level:** Ultrathink` header in each of four workflow files. Both read as configuration the skill applies per mode — but on Opus 5 thinking is adaptive and always on, with depth set by `effort`. Nothing in a skill body can set a thinking level, so the column promised a mode that does not exist.

`ck-code-review`'s "Ultrathink to exhaustively list ALL…" and "Think harder to scan…" are a weaker case: as bare imperatives they still parse as ordinary instructions, just redundant. Cleaned up while in the files.

**Deliberately left alone:** `ck-debug/references/systematic-debugging.md:82`. It sits under *"Human Partner Signals You're Doing It Wrong"* and lists things the **user** says — "Ultrathink this" beside "Stop guessing" and "We're stuck?". A recognition cue, not a mode setting; deleting it would remove a signal the debugger reads.

Adding `effort:` to skill frontmatter is **not** the replacement. It is schema-valid and would pass tier0, but no shipped skill sets it, it cannot express bootstrap's four per-mode values from one frontmatter block, and adopting an untested mechanism inside a deletion ships a behavior change in disguise. Worth proposing separately, with an eval.

## The item that induces fabrication

`coding-level-4-lead.md` said **"MUST quantify everything possible (latency, throughput, cost, effort)"** for every response at that level. That invites numbers the model has not measured — precisely the failure `opus-5-calibration.md` §4 describes, since Opus 5 states unsure things confidently. A fabricated latency figure in an executive summary is worse than an admitted unknown.

Now scoped to what there is a measurement or cited source for, with "say a number is unknown rather than estimating one". The mandatory likelihood×impact matrix applies when the decision has risks worth ranking. `docs-manager`'s coverage-percentage metric is conditional on a coverage tool having actually run, for the same reason.

Five templates also get **one byte-identical sentence** above their section list — scale to the size of the work, drop empty sections rather than emitting empty headings. Identical wording on purpose: `grep -rc opus-5-calibration claude/agents/ claude/output-styles/` is then the coverage check, which per-file bespoke prose would not give you.

`journal-writer` got the lighter touch — its 200–500 word range became a target rather than a floor, with no clause. Journal entries are reflective prose where a length bar is a plausible deliberate choice rather than scale-blindness, so it is the one file here where the range itself was worth keeping.

**Skeletons stay.** They are the artifact contract `_shared/references/workflow-artifacts.md` and cook's finalize step reason about; deleting them breaks consumers. Levels 3 and 5 are untouched — L3 already forbids padding, L5 is terse by design, and editing them for symmetry would be churn against the progressive-level design.

## Doc drift

- **README** advertised multi-provider notifications, GitHub Actions, and CI/CD, and pointed at `.claude/hooks/notifications/docs/`. Confirmed `hooks/notifications/` is in `metadata.json`'s deletions list and neither it nor `.github/` exists, then deleted the section.
- **`eval/README.md` + `eval/run.py`** both pinned `claude-opus-4-8` as the example baseline. `run.py` has no hardcoded default, so only the docs were stale — but a doc telling you to pin an older model is how stale baselines get created. Both updated, with a note that results captured on an earlier model are not comparable across the switch.
- **`runtime-awareness.md`** documented `AUTOCOMPACT_BUFFER = 45000` where the code has `40000`. Fixed the doc, not the code: the constant is read only on the fallback branch taken when the harness omits `used_percentage`, and the window size is harness-supplied. The "22.5% reserved" figure was arithmetic against an assumed 200K window and is dropped rather than recomputed.
- **`repomix/SKILL.md`** listed Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-3.5 as context-limit examples.

## Verification

```
python3 eval/tier0_static.py     # 2 pass, 0 fail
npm test                          # 939 tests, 0 fail
npm run test:statusline           # 4 suites, 0 failed
```

Green after every batch. Two guards were load-bearing rather than incidental:

- `advisory-boundary-policy.test.cjs` regexes the **`--fast` row** of the bootstrap mode table and asserts three other substrings in that file — dropping a column shifts every cell in every row, so the change was checked against it rather than assumed safe. Column counts verified at 5 across all rows afterward.
- The same test asserts two substrings in `code-reviewer.md` and **forbids** two others. A naive scale-down sentence mentioning task completion would have failed it; confirmed the guarded phrases survive and the forbidden ones were not introduced.

Two review-checklist greps came back non-zero and were **checked rather than acted on** — `statusline-string-utils.cjs:115` uses `45000` as a duration-format example in milliseconds, and `README:487` is a Discord community link, not the removed notification feature. Both stay.

## Still deferred

The `Task` → `Agent` prose sweep (76 refs, ~30 files). The alias still works in 2.1.226, so nothing is broken. If ever done: restrict to `Task tool`, `Task(subagent_type=`, and "zero Task calls" — a global replace would corrupt `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate`, `extractTaskListId`, and plan-template "TODO tasks" — and it must not touch `claude/hooks/` or `claude/settings.json`. New text in both PRs already uses `Agent`.

items.title: v0.9.112 — FFI-boundary hardening + Tokio-runtime sanity clamp + MPI-aware thread pools
items.body:
# v0.9.112 — FFI-boundary hardening + Tokio-runtime sanity clamp + MPI-aware thread pools

Three independent hardening streams in one release. They share a version bump because they landed together on the same working branch and each one alone is small enough that a mid-release cut would have felt worse than a slightly larger release.

## What's in this PR

- **FFI-boundary hardening** — closes [#161][161] (error chains dropped at the PyO3 boundary) and [#162][162] (MultiEndpointStore explicit per-endpoint pinning), which together are the direct fix for `mlcommons/storage#755`'s symptom.
- **Tokio-runtime sanity clamp on `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS`** — closes an under-provisioning class of bug that turned the DLIO unet3d datagen benchmark into a 1-worker Tokio runtime and cost ~9× throughput at NP=1.
- **MPI-aware thread-pool auto-init at import time** — every s3dlio-owned pool (global Tokio runtime, checkpoint runtime, Rayon global, dgen-rs recommended-threads) now sizes to `num_cpus / world_size` without any downstream opt-in.

[161]: https://github.com/russfellows/s3dlio/issues/161
[162]: https://github.com/russfellows/s3dlio/issues/162

---

## 1. FFI-boundary hardening (mlcommons/storage#755, s3dlio#161, s3dlio#162)

**Motivation.** A DLIO training run against S3 died with only:

```
RuntimeError: concurrent range chunk failed
```

No indication of what actually went wrong on the wire. Root cause, filed as [#161][161]: error conversion at the PyO3 boundary used `Display` (`{}`) on `anyhow::Error` values, which shows only the outermost `.context(...)` label and discards the full cause chain.

### Tier 1 — error-chain preservation (25+ sites)

All error-conversion sites across `python_core_api.rs` (19 sites), `python_aiml_api.rs` (checkpoint sites), `python_advanced_api.rs` (`MultipartUploadWriter`), and `python_datagen_api.rs` (1 site — previously hand-rolled `{:#}` formatting, now routed through the same shared `py_err()` helper for consistency) now preserve the full `anyhow` cause chain via `error_chain_message()` (`{:#}` alternate `Display`) instead of collapsing to the top-level context label.

**Direct effect on storage#755.** The same `RuntimeError: concurrent range chunk failed` failure will now include the real SDK / timeout / TLS / etc. cause in its message. Note: this improves diagnosability, not resilience — a run that previously failed under the same conditions will still fail, just with the real cause now visible.

### Tier 2 — `checksum()` fix

Extracted `snapshot_final_writer_stats()` as a pure, GIL-free helper so the checksum-after-finalize behavior is unit-testable.

### Tier 3 — bucket-swallow + etag fixes, multipart writer pinning

- `MultipartUploadWriter.reserve()` now takes `PyRefMut<'_, Self>` instead of `&mut self` so the writer object is pinned alive for the duration of a `reserve()` … `commit()` cycle.
- `close()` always populates the `"etag"` key in its result dict, even on the no-op / already-closed path.

### Tier 4 — second-round FFI hardening (5 items)

1. `exists()` / `exists_async()` docstrings now explain that both collapse every failure mode to `False` by design (mirrors `os.path.exists()`), and point callers who need to distinguish "not found" from "couldn't check" at `stat()`. No logic change.
2. Unknown-length ("iterable-style") datasets now raise `TypeError` from `PyDataset.__len__`, `PyBytesAsyncDataLoader.__iter__`/`.items()`, and `PyBytesAsyncDataLoaderIter.spawn_stream` instead of silently defaulting to empty/0. No currently Python-constructible dataset type can trigger this path today — closes a latent trap, not a live behavior break.
3. Migrated 7 of 9 writer `block_on()` call sites (all 4 `create_*_writer` functions, `finalize()`, `write_owned_bytes()`) to the established `submit_io()` / `run_on_global_rt()` pattern, closing a reentrancy-panic risk. `write_chunk()`'s 2 sites are deliberately left on `block_on()` — its zero-copy fast path holds a borrowed `PyBuffer` slice that can't cross a `'static`-future boundary without a copy.
4. Switched 3 sync-iterator classes from `std::sync::Mutex` to `parking_lot::Mutex` so a prior unrelated panic in an iteration callback no longer permanently wedges the iterator via poisoning.
5. `python_datagen_api.rs:410` `generate_npz_bytes` error path now routes through `py_err()` (the last Tier 4 hand-rolled `{:#}` holdout).

### #162 — MultiEndpointStore explicit per-endpoint pinning

New public methods: `get_from_endpoint`, `put_to_endpoint`, `delete_from_endpoint`, `put_all_endpoints`, `list_all_endpoints`. These sit alongside the existing round-robin / least-connections load-balancing so callers who need explicit per-endpoint targeting (e.g. checkpoint sharding across specific replicas) don't have to fight the balancer.

### Test-suite hygiene

- Deleted stale `test_checkpoint_basic.py` (dead API, superseded duplicate).
- Full audit of `python/tests/` to eliminate the `return True/False` test-masking anti-pattern.

### FFI hardening: design docs

See `docs/DESIGN_FFI_BOUNDARY_HARDENING.md` and `docs/DESIGN_TIER4_FFI_HARDENING.md` for the full per-item design rationale and decisions.

---

## 2. Tokio-runtime sanity clamp on `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS`

**Motivation.** The DLIO unet3d datagen benchmark ceilinged at ~214 MB/s per rank while isolated s3dlio benchmarks against the same target hit 2500 MB/s per rank — same code path, same wire, 10× throughput gap. Root-caused to:

DLIO's `dlio_benchmark/storage/obj_store_lib.py` `ObjStoreLibStorage.__init__` computes:

```python
_rt_threads = min(_write_threads * 3 // 2, 128)
os.environ["S3DLIO_RT_THREADS"] = str(_rt_threads)
```

With Hydra's default `write_threads: int = 1` (unet3d_datagen workload does not override), that resolves to `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS=1`. Pre-0.9.112 s3dlio faithfully obeyed the env var and built the global Tokio runtime with **one** worker. Every concurrent MPU part upload then serialized through that one worker: p50 `close()` latency = 22 843 ms per file, aggregate throughput ~214 MB/s per rank.

**Fix.** `get_runtime_threads()` (`src/s3_client.rs`) and `effective_thread_budget()` (`src/constants.rs`, used by the checkpoint runtime and dgen-rs paths) now share `clamped_env_rt_threads()`: if `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS` is set and is below `RT_THREADS_LIMIT / 4` (the per-process target set by `configure_thread_pools`, auto-called at import time to the MPI-aware auto-budget), the env var is treated as downstream miscomputation and replaced with `RT_THREADS_LIMIT`. A stderr warning is printed the first time the clamp fires so operators can spot the underlying miscomputation. `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS_UNSAFE=1` bypasses the clamp for legitimate low-thread scenarios (single-threaded test suites, fault injection).

### Live before/after (real s3-ultra target, NP=1, 40 × 146 MB files)

| Metric               | Pre-fix (0.9.110)  | Post-fix (this PR)  |
| -------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- |
| Wall time            | 27.4 s             | **2.9 s**           |
| Throughput           | 214 MB/s           | **~1928 MB/s** (9×) |
| Upload `close()` p50 | 22 843 ms          | **309 ms** (77×)    |
| Upload `close()` p99 | 26 368 ms          | 529 ms              |
| Rt-worker threads    | 1                  | 28 (= LIMIT)        |

Cross-backend live smoke test with `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS=1` forced: `file://` 397 MB/s, `direct://` (on `/mnt/nvme_data`) 655 MB/s, `s3://` (s3-ultra) 919 MB/s. `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS_UNSAFE=1` correctly re-enables the pathological 1-worker behavior for testing. Sane values (e.g. `S3DLIO_RT_THREADS=16`) pass through unchanged, no warning, 1.1 GB/s.

Full investigation writeup: `docs/investigation/DLIO_UNET3D_DATAGEN_BOTTLENECK_INVESTIGATION_2026-07-10.md`.

---

## 3. MPI-aware thread-pool auto-init at import time

The `_pymod` init hook now calls `s3_client::configure_thread_pools(0)` before registering any Python functions. This sets `RT_THREADS_LIMIT` to the MPI-aware per-process budget (`num_cpus / world_size`, floor 1) and builds Rayon's global pool at the same target — every s3dlio Python import, no explicit call needed. Closes the CPU-oversubscription class of bug where N ranks on the same host each independently defaulted to `num_cpus` threads.

New helpers in `src/constants.rs`:
- `mpi_world_size()` — reads `OMPI_COMM_WORLD_SIZE` / `PMI_SIZE` / `WORLD_SIZE`
- `mpi_aware_thread_budget()` — the shared per-process formula
- `effective_thread_budget()` — single-knob sizing used by the checkpoint runtime and `hardware::recommended_data_gen_threads()`

`get_runtime_threads()` folds MPI-awareness into its default fallback; `configure_thread_pools()` is the single choke point for setting `RT_THREADS_LIMIT`, the pyo3-async-runtimes Tokio init, and Rayon's global pool. `configure_tokio_threads()` in `python_aiml_api.rs` now delegates to it.

---

## RED-then-GREEN test evidence (thread-pool bugfix)

Added in `src/s3_client.rs` `mpi_aware_runtime_sizing_tests` (11 tests):
- MPI-aware default, single-process default, env-var override precedence, LIMIT-caps-default, auto-set-from-MPI, explicit-count-override, idempotent-repeat-calls
- `get_runtime_threads_clamps_grossly_underprovisioned_env_var_up_to_limit` — the DLIO regression

- `get_runtime_threads_unsafe_env_bypasses_the_clamp` — escape hatch
- `get_runtime_threads_env_var_low_with_no_limit_set_is_honored` — pure-Rust programmatic use unaffected

- Same shape for the checkpoint-runtime / dgen-rs path.

Added in `src/hardware.rs` (2 tests):
- `recommended_data_gen_threads_honors_explicit_thread_budget_when_no_override`
- `recommended_data_gen_threads_explicit_override_still_wins`

Added in `src/python_api/python_aiml_api.rs` (1 timing-based test):
- `build_checkpoint_runtime_honors_explicit_thread_budget`

All RED-verified against pre-fix code, all pass under the fix.
