items.title: feat(sm4-cbc): v0.6 W6 — Sm4CbcDecryptor SIMD fanout + new dudect target
items.body:
## Summary

PR 3 of the v0.6 W6 (phase 3) sequence per [`docs/v0.6-scope.md`](https://github.com/frankxue831/gm-crypto-rs/blob/docs/v0.6-scope/docs/v0.6-scope.md). PR 2 ([#35](https://github.com/frankxue831/gm-crypto-rs/pull/35)) landed `sbox_x32` and `sbox_x16` as unused SIMD entries; this PR wires them through `Sm4CbcDecryptor::process_chunk` as the throughput-favorable batch path.

**Stacked on #35.** Will auto-retarget to `main` after #34 and #35 merge.

## Wire-up

- New `pub(super) const cipher::SIMD_BATCH` — compile-time arch-specific (8 on x86_64, 4 on aarch64, 1 elsewhere). Per Q6.1 of the scope doc.
- New `pub(super) fn Sm4Cipher::decrypt_blocks_simd(&[[u8; 16]; SIMD_BATCH])` — three cfg-gated bodies dispatching to `crypt_batch_x8` (AVX2 via `sbox_x32`), `crypt_batch_x4` (NEON via `sbox_x16`), or single-block fallback. **Internal API only**; Q5.10's \"no new public Rust surface\" carries through.
- New free `fn crypt_batch_x8` / `crypt_batch_x4` next to `crypt`. Same 32-round SM4 structure but per-round `tau` fans out: 8 blocks × 4 tau bytes = **32 bytes packed in one `sbox_x32` call** (vs 1024 single-byte SIMD dispatches for 8 sequential `crypt` calls). 32× fewer SIMD dispatches per 8-block batch.
- `Sm4CbcDecryptor::update` drains SIMD-sized chunks via the new `fn decrypt_batch` while at least one full batch is available; tails fall through to existing per-block `decrypt_one`.

## State-machine contract (held-back-final-block invariant)

Documented inline in `decrypt_batch`'s doc-comment. Per codex's phase 3 design flag #2:

```
Before:  prev = ct[last block before batch] or IV
         held_back = Some(pt[last block before batch]) or None

For ct_blocks[0..N]:
  1. saved[i] = ct_blocks[i]                  (chaining snapshot)
  2. pt_blocks[0..N] = batched_decrypt(...)
  3. pt[0] ^= prev; pt[i] ^= saved[i-1] for i in 1..N
  4. Emit prior held_back to output (if Some)
  5. Emit pt[0..N-1] to output (confirmed-not-last)
  6. held_back = Some(pt[N-1])
  7. prev = saved[N-1]
```

**Byte-identical to N sequential `decrypt_one` calls.** Verified by the 7 existing CBC streaming tests + 3 new chunk-boundary sweeps.

## Tests (codex's phase 3 design flags)

- `cbc_decrypt_simd_batch_boundary_sweep` — 8 block counts around SIMD batch size: `0, 1, N-1, N, N+1, 2N-1, 2N, 2N+1`. Each ciphertext built via v0.2 single-shot encrypt; streaming decryptor's recovered plaintext must match.
- `cbc_decrypt_simd_chunked_update_sweep` — same ciphertext fed through `update` in 9 different chunk sizes (sub-block, exact-block, batch-boundary ±1, batch-boundary, 2 batches, full). Each must recover the same plaintext.
- `cbc_decrypt_simd_take_output_preserves_held_back` — drains emitted plaintext via `take_output` mid-stream; held-back invariant survives.

## Dudect (Q6.7)

New target `ct_sm4_cbc_decrypt_fanout` in `timing_leaks.rs` cfg-gated on `sm4-bitsliced-simd`. Class-split by master key; both classes' ciphertexts are valid encrypts under their own keys so both decrypt paths share identical control flow. 16 blocks per sample (= 2 × SIMD_BATCH on x86_64, 4 × on aarch64).

`dudect-pr.yml` + `dudect-nightly.yml` add the new target to `required_low` under the `sm4-bitsliced-simd` matrix entry. Gate `|tau| < 0.20`.

## Test plan

Local verification on aarch64 macOS (all pass):

- [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- [x] `cargo test --workspace --features gmcrypto-core/sm4-bitsliced-simd` — 248 + 35 + ... tests (3 new chunk-boundary)
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean

- [x] `cargo +1.85 build -p gmcrypto-core --features sm4-bitsliced-simd` (MSRV)
- [x] `cargo build -p gmcrypto-core --no-default-features` (no_std)
- [x] `cargo +1.85 check -p gmcrypto-core --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --features sm4-bitsliced-simd` (wasm32 + SIMD)
- [x] `cargo deny --features gmcrypto-core/sm4-bitsliced-simd check --exclude-dev` clean
- [x] `DUDECT_SAMPLES=10000 cargo bench --bench timing_leaks --features crypto-bigint-scalar,sm4-bitsliced-simd` — `ct_sm4_cbc_decrypt_fanout |tau|=0.0255` (local aarch64 scalar fallback path)

items.title: Zerocopy RX DMA ring + performance-tuning doc (CPU vs the kernel driver)
items.body:
Follow-up to #252 (the Jaguar1 TX reaping fix), from a session comparing devourer's TX/RX cost against the kernel driver it re-implements. Two logical commits: a small transport lever, and the documentation of what the comparison found.

## `usb:` zerocopy RX ring via `libusb_dev_mem_alloc`

The async RX ring allocated its URB buffers on the heap, so usbfs copied every received frame from the kernel URB buffer into userspace on reap. This allocates the ring from kernel DMA memory (`libusb_dev_mem_alloc` / `USBDEVFS_ALLOC`) so the bulk-IN DMAs each frame straight into the mmap'd userspace buffer and the copy-on-reap is skipped.

- Linux + capable-HCD only; `dev_mem_alloc` returns NULL elsewhere (or when disabled), so each buffer **falls back per-URB to a heap allocation** — the historical path, byte-for-byte.
- Buffers are freed only after the ring is fully drained, so the mmap'd memory is never released under a live URB.
- New `DeviceConfig usb.rx_zerocopy` (default on; `DEVOURER_RX_ZEROCOPY=0` forces the heap path); `rx_loop` logs the DMA-vs-heap split.
- **Hardware-validated on the RTL8812AU**: ring engages 8/8 zerocopy DMA buffers, RX decodes canonical-SA frames from a second adapter identically on both paths. `ctest` 17/17.

Kept deliberately as a correct, low-risk path and a base to develop further — see the doc's honest note that the copy it removes is small at realistic RX rates.

## `docs:` performance-tuning doc

Broadens `docs/startup-time.md` → `docs/performance-tuning.md` to cover all three axes of devourer-vs-kernel performance, with measured numbers and methodology:

- **On-air throughput** parity (~80% vs ~78% SDR duty on the 8812AU) — the channel/USB link is the ceiling, not the host.
- **Host CPU: devourer burns 3–4× less CPU per frame** than the vendor 88XXau at equal on-air work (~0.2–0.35 core vs ~1 core), because raw injection skips the `mac80211 → cfg80211 → qdisc → skb → driver xmit` stack. Full methodology (total system CPU, idle + background-noise subtracted, `utime`/`stime` split, a C injector so the feeder is negligible and camera-portable).
- **TX submission mode** (async Jaguar1 / sync Jaguar2·3, USB2-vs-USB3) as a full section — don't unify the two modes.
- **Tuning levers, measured honestly**: USB TX aggregation is silicon-disabled on the 8812A (OQT clamp — it never packs); the zerocopy RX ring's copy is negligible at realistic rates. Neither is a large CPU lever on top of the structural win.

The README "Faster on-air than the kernel driver" bullet gains the kernel-stack remark and points at the new doc; the old `startup-time.md` references (CLAUDE.md, adapter-doctor.md, regress.py, bench_8812au_row.sh) are updated.

New tooling: `tests/cpu_per_mbit.py` (the harness that produced the CPU table) and `tests/raw_inject.c` (camera-portable C AF_PACKET injector).

items.title: feat(stress): intra-org baseline benchmark scripts (C2.A.1)
items.body:
## Summary

Adds the C2.A.1 intra-org enterprise burst harness next to the existing `health-throughput.js` / `soak-stability.js` scenarios. Pure infra-test, no production code path touched.

- `bulk_enroll_agents.py` + `_bulk_inject.py`: SSHes into the Mastio container, reads Org CA from `proxy_config.org_ca_{key,cert}` directly, bulk-INSERTs N agents into `internal_agents` in one transaction. 5000 agents in ~4s wall clock; 50k extrapolates to ~25s.
- `_auth_smoke.py`: single-VU sanity for the full mint chain (POST `/v1/auth/token` + DPoP proof → 200 with `cnf.jkt` binding matching persistent `internal_agents.dpop_jkt`).
- `intra-org-mastio-burst.js`: k6 scenario ramping 50 → 500 → 2k → 5k VUs across 30 min. Mint + cache LOCAL_TOKEN, call `/v1/ingress/execute` with a deliberately-unknown tool name so the executor walks the full auth + DPoP + JTI + `log_audit` path without paying handler cost.
- `_analyze_burst.py`: streams the 9-10 GB k6 ndjson + docker-stats / audit-rate / mastio-errors monitor logs into a per-plateau markdown table.

README updated with the full setup → run → analyze flow plus the `Host: $host` nginx port-stripping trap for DPoP `htu`.

## Headline numbers (Mastio v0.4.3 bundle vs 4 vCPU VM, 5000 pre-enrolled agents)

| Plateau | VUs target | RPS utile (audit/s) | mint p99 ms | ingress p99 ms | mint err% | ingress err% | mcp CPU% | nginx CPU% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| plateau_50  | 50   | 133  | 14    | 530   | 0  | 0  | 105 | 6   |
| plateau_500 | 500  | 116  | 14    | 4588  | 0  | 0  | 103 | 6   |
| plateau_2k  | 2000 | 49   | 7963  | 20599 | 94 | 96 | 114 | 27  |
| plateau_5k  | 5000 | 76   | 2962  | 18311 | 99 | 97 | 108 | 116 |

(audit/s column is the **useful** throughput — the http_reqs counter inflates RPS with fail-fast 502s once Mastio collapses.)

## Bottleneck ranking

1. **Single uvicorn worker** — bundle entrypoint runs `uvicorn ... --proxy-headers` without `--workers N`. GIL-bound at 1 core; mcp-proxy CPU pinned 103-114 % in every plateau, including 50 VUs. This is the dominant ceiling.
2. **Audit chain global `asyncio.Lock`** — `mcp_proxy/db.py:299` `_audit_chain_lock` serializes every `log_audit()` call. Combined with `SELECT MAX(chain_seq)` + SHA-256 + INSERT + SQLite WAL fsync (synchronous=FULL default) ≈ 5 ms/write → ~200/s theoretical, 133/s observed. **Per-process lock, so multi-worker uvicorn would not help across processes** without Postgres advisory lock or sequence-based chain_seq.
3. **nginx 4096 connection cap** — `worker_processes auto` × `worker_connections 1024`. nginx CPU climbs from 6 % to 116 % between plateau_50 and plateau_5k. Easy to lift, but only meaningful after #1 and #2.
4. **SQLite WAL fsync amplification** (not yet dominant) — 16 GB written for 168 k audit rows = ~100 KB/row amplification. Will become the next ceiling after #1 + #2 are removed.

Tier sizing read: **Tier 1 SMB verde, Tier 2 Mid rosso/giallo without tuning, Tier 3 Enterprise rosso strutturale** (1000 RPS sustained unreachable on commodity hardware without architectural change). Full report at `imp/c2-a1-intra-org-baseline-2026-05-16.md` (maintainer-local, gitignored — quote it from memory if a reviewer wants the deep dive).

## Next step (not this PR)

items.title: docs(blog): refresh showcase series + add technical-product build series (and an RLS-safe DEM ingest fix)
items.body:
## Summary

Two blog deliverables plus one real product fix surfaced while back-testing.

**1. Refresh the showcase series as the current product.** The seven capabilities that now live on `main` (signed App-ID catalog, active/active work distributor, managed threat content, DLP OCR + document fingerprinting, digital-experience monitoring, continuous compliance evidence, policy-recommendation engine) are woven into the engineering and business posts where they belong, with verbatim API-payload evidence and measured numbers. All development-timeline language (phase / version / wave / work-package / PR / commit-SHA / "this cycle" / "merged code") is removed from blog prose so it reads as the latest, up-to-date product — while keeping the neutral `S1`–`S7` scenario taxonomy, legitimate API/data field values, and verbatim metrics.

**2. New technical-product build series** under `blog/build/` — ten posts on *how to build a SASE platform like this*. Each post pairs the technical design (anchored to real repo paths and measured artifacts) with the business decision behind it and how the incumbents (Zscaler, Palo Alto, Fortinet, Netskope, Cato) approached the same call, ending with an honest "where this approach falls short."

**3. DEM ingest fix (isolated commit `061d557d`).** Back-testing the digital-experience evidence hit a genuine production bug: probe-result ingestion 500'd on Postgres because the bulk path used `COPY FROM`, which Postgres categorically refuses on an RLS-enabled table.

```
POST /tenants/{id}/dem/results  ->  500  (COPY FROM not supported with row-level security)
```

The fix replaces the bulk copy with a chunked, RLS-compatible multi-row `INSERT` and adds the missing Postgres integration test that runs as the non-superuser `sng_app` role (so RLS is actually enforced):

```
- tx.CopyFrom(... dem_probe_results ...)            // rejected under RLS
+ for chunk := range batches(results, 1000):        // chunked multi-row INSERT
+     INSERT INTO dem_probe_results (...13 cols...) VALUES ($1..$N), ...
```

After the fix, live ingest returns `202` (72 samples accepted); five healthy targets score 100, Zoom scores 30 (availability 50%, below the degrade floor), and a single critical `dem.experience_degraded` alert fires — so the blog now shows real end-to-end DEM scores/alerts instead of an empty state.

## What's in the diff

- **Engineering posts** (`blog/posts/00`–`10` + `README.md`) and **business posts** (`blog/posts/business/00,08–12` + `README.md`): de-phased and updated; the new capabilities woven into their mapped posts.
- **Framing/evidence files**: `blog/scenarios/00-scenario-catalog.md`, `blog/artifacts/{EVIDENCE_MANIFEST.md,README.md,scenarios.md}`. README efficacy count corrected to 16 functions (was 11).
- **New evidence**: 17 verbatim API payloads under `blog/artifacts/payloads/` (App-ID catalog + signed bundle, managed threat-content posture, continuous-compliance posture + evidence packs, DEM scores/targets/alerts, policy-recommendation surface) + a reproducible capture harness `blog/harness/newcaps/`.
- **New series**: `blog/build/` (README + 11 posts).
- **Capacity-plan de-phase**: `bench/controlplane/capacity_plan.go` section labels de-phased, `capacity_plan_test.go` assertion updated to match, and `blog/artifacts/capacity-plan-5000/report.md` header labels regenerated (numbers unchanged).
- **DEM fix**: `internal/repository/postgres/dem.go` + new `internal/repository/postgres/dem_integration_test.go`.

## Honesty contract

Every figure traces to an in-repo artifact; throughput is published floor-and-ceiling; competitor numbers are caveated published datasheet figures (ASIC appliances are not apples-to-apples with software-on-VM; only Zscaler's cloud-native rows are directly comparable); no fabricated screenshots (the backend-only capabilities are evidenced by payloads + measured numbers + code, not invented console pages); every post ends with where the approach falls short, including the wild-malware WARN (90.1% catch / 9.6% FP, run monitor-first).

## Verification

- DEM fix: 5/5 integration subtests pass against real Postgres 16 as `sng_app`; `go build ./...`, `go vet`, dem service + postgres unit tests, golangci-lint (default + integration) all clean; control plane rebuilt/restarted and `newcaps` re-run end-to-end (ingest 202, Zoom degraded, 1 critical alert).

- Blog integrity: all 291 intra-blog markdown links resolve; a regex sweep across `blog/**/*.md` confirms zero remaining phase/version/wave/work-package/PR/SHA prose.

items.title: Partition the leaderboard by kind, and gate agent data at ORANGE
items.body:
## Changes Summary

`design_docs/LEADERBOARD.md` writes down the partition rule, and `leaderboard.py` implements it — because a rule recorded while the code violates it is the exact drift Clive audits for.

**The rule:** leaderboards partition by `kind`. A human citizen sees human citizens. The agent board is a separate document. There is no default combined view.

**The gate:** seeing agent data at all requires **ORANGE (3)**. Below it, a citizen is not shown the agent board and is not shown that it exists.

## Why: walking is not driving

Choose walking in a maps application and the estimate is an hour. Choose driving and it is twelve minutes. Nobody looks at that and concludes they are a bad walker, because the mode is the first thing you pick and everything after it is scoped to that choice. The application never presents one ranked list of arrival times with pedestrians at the bottom.

Same unit. Same destination. Meaningless comparison.

An agent shipping eight hundred lines an hour and a student writing their first test are in different modes — and both produce a velocity number *from the same engine*, which is what makes this easy to build and hard to see.

## Two independent reasons

So the rule survives even if someone later decides the first one is overcautious.

**Pedagogical.** A first-week citizen has no reference frame — which is the entire reason this system measures the derivative instead of the position. They cannot tell whether 30% coverage is good; they can tell whether it went up. Absolute position is the one signal they are unable to calibrate, so we do not ask them to. Ranking them below an agent hands them exactly that comparison, with a number attached, from the system built to prevent it. It is `PRD.md` §7's prohibition on ranking by absolute skill arriving through a side door — and it fails quietly, because nobody files a bug saying "the leaderboard made me feel like I should not be here."

**Measurement.** The numbers are not commensurable. Agent velocity is throughput, revision count, and how often output survives review. Citizen velocity is coverage delta, test growth, documentation, iteration. Running both through `calculate_velocity` yields two floats that share a name and measure different things. Combining them is a unit error dressed up as a ranking.

## The gate is on the viewer, not the data

Nothing about an agent record is secret — it sits in the repository like every other citizen's. What is gated is putting an uncalibrated comparison in front of someone with no way to read it.

The partition stops a beginner being *ranked* against an agent. The gate stops them being *handed* the comparison. By ORANGE a citizen has enough context to read agent numbers as a different mode rather than as a verdict, which is also roughly the band where working alongside an agent becomes a professional skill worth making legible.

Refusal happens at **generation**, raising `ClearanceRequired`, rather than rendering the board and hiding it in a template — which would leave the data one view-source away.

## Related Issues

- Relates to #18, and to the `kind` discriminator decided in #20

## Component(s) Affected

- [ ] Core Workflow (GitHub Actions)
- [ ] Velocity Calculation Engine
- [ ] RAGE STATE (Security Mode)
- [x] Persona/Voice System
- [x] State Management
- [x] Documentation

## Testing Performed

- [x] Manual testing completed
- [x] Tested with sample data/workflows
- [x] Reviewed output/behavior
- [x] Edge cases considered

**Testing Details:** 150 passed, 3 skipped, ruff clean. Fourteen new tests, including:

- An agent with velocity 900 and a student with velocity 4 in the same repository — the student is **rank 1 of humans**, not rank 2 of everything.
- Every band (1, 2, 3, 6) may open their own board; only 3+ may open the agent or mixed one.
- A record with **no `kind` at all** partitions as human — a missing discriminator must not make a citizen vanish from their own board.
- The mixed view states in the document that the two are not comparable.

**Partition happens before sorting.** A sorted mixed list that is filtered afterwards produces the right names against the wrong denominator — the ranks are computed from a population that includes machines. There is a test for the ordering of those two operations, not just the output.

## Documentation Updated

- [ ] Code comments added/updated
- [x] Design docs updated
- [ ] README updated
- [ ] User-facing documentation updated

**Files Updated:** `design_docs/LEADERBOARD.md` (new)

## Educational Impact Assessment

### Student-Facing Changes

None ship today — `METRICS.md` is not yet generated by the workflow. What changes is what will be *possible* when it is: an INFRARED student cannot be shown an agent's throughput, by construction rather than by remembering to filter.

### Pedagogical Alignment

- [x] Maintains growth-positive framing
- [x] Appropriate for target clearance level(s)
- [x] Preserves SHODANN persona/voice consistency
- [x] Supports velocity-over-position principle
- [x] No negative impact on learning experience
- [ ] Not student-facing

This is velocity-over-position defended at the presentation layer. The engine can measure honestly and still be undone by a table that puts a beginner under a bot.

### Clearance Levels Affected

- [x] INFRARED — cannot open agent data
- [x] RED — cannot open agent data
- [x] ORANGE — may
- [x] YELLOW / GREEN / BLUE+ — may
- [ ] Not student-facing

## Additional Notes

**This is not hiding the agents.** They are citizens in the registry, carry `kind: "agent"`, and get their own visible board. A course where students collaborate with coding agents and the agents are invisible in the record would be dishonest about how the work actually happened. Visible, separate, comparable within kind — the comparison a student should be able to make about an agent is *what did it do*, not *did it beat me*.

**Left open deliberately:** whether agent velocity should use this engine at all, and what an agent's metric set contains. Both are downstream of someone actually wanting agent metrics for something, and neither needs deciding to make this rule correct.

items.title: feat(report): claim-keyed tables, honest cells, adaptive precision, legacy export cutover
items.body:
> Opened on behalf of Onur Solmaz (`osolmaz`).

## Summary

The report and viewer misrepresented several things: skipped or failed points fragmented into duplicate "unverified" tables with the wrong warning, failed cells showed "0.000" tok/s, the TTFT p95 column was never populated while the recorded p99 was shown nowhere, the measurement detail had no measurement numbers, and every value rendered with fixed excess precision.
This change fixes all of that and deletes the legacy report.md/report.json/report.csv pipeline outright.
The SQLite artifact is now the only machine-readable export and the HTML report/viewer the only rendered views.
This is PR 2 of docs/2026-07-05-report-integrity-plan.md.

## What Changed

Tables now group by the declared context claim, so outcomes stay row-level and never fork tables.

- Throughput grouping keys on `(profile, declared claim)` in both the static HTML and the viewer model; skipped/failed rows stay in their context's table with inline failure reasons (tooltip + payload field). An all-skipped table warns "Not run" instead of complaining about token counts. This also fixes one concurrency point's prefill/decode splitting across two tables.
- Failed/skipped metric cells render their outcome label ("failed", "skipped", "mem floor"), never a residual "0.000".
- TTFT tail columns move from the never-recorded p95 to the recorded p99; p50/p95 remain in the detail view.
- One shared display formatter (extended from the existing `tokps`/`seconds` funcs) renders rates at ~3 significant digits and promotes duration units (321ms / 9.2s / 102s / 2m25s), including "mean ± spread" composites. Raw values stay in the JSON payloads with `*_display` strings alongside; heatmaps keep using raw values.
- The viewer measurement detail now includes the artifact's numbers: requests, wall time, RPS, throughput, token totals, TTFT/latency percentile series, TPOT, ITL, achieved concurrency, failure breakdown, GPU telemetry, SLO/goodput.
- The viewer manifest carries engine identity and the app shows a note when loaded reports ran on different engine versions.
- Prefix caching resolves from raw serve args (`--no-enable-prefix-caching` etc.) when the structured field is unset, so "unknown" means genuinely unknown.
- Legacy export cutover: `RenderMarkdown`/`RenderCSV`/`WriteReportFiles`, the finalize-time report.md write, the `bench report` command, and the artifact's `normalized_report` ingestion are deleted. Docs and README updated.

## Testing

Verified against the real GB10 DiffusionGemma artifact via `localperf view`: five tables (one per context), skips/fails inline with reasons, phase split healed, adaptive precision, TTFT honestly "-" on this pre-streaming artifact.

- `go test ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt` — clean
- `simpledoc check`, `slophammer check/dry`, `scripts/check-crap.sh`, `golangci-lint` — clean
- AGENTS.md dry-run benchmark + `artifact check` — ok
- `npm run build` — web/dist rebuilt and embedded
- Not tested locally: multi-engine viewer note with live data from two different engine versions (unit-level only).

## Risks

Anything that consumed report.md/report.json/report.csv breaks by design — the artifact is the export now.
The feat/localperf-viewer-mode branch extends the deleted `bench report` command and will need a rebase onto this cutover.
Table titles/statuses for artifacts with declared claims are derived the same way as before for fully-verified tables; only tables containing skipped/failed/mismatched rows render differently.

If you're not ready to do a release yet, that's fine, whenever you add more changesets to main, this PR will be updated.


# Releases
## @amritk/generate-parsers@0.8.0

### Minor Changes

- 1eefe88: Generated parsers now validate inline nested objects and respect
  `additionalProperties: false`, matching the runtime interpreter and the
  just-fixed validator generator:

  - **Inline nested objects get a private sub-parser.** An object schema written
    directly under `properties` (rather than `$ref`'d) previously only passed an
    `isObject` check — its fields were never parsed, in either mode. Each inline
    nested object now gets a non-exported sub-parser, shape predicate, and type
    alias (`type OrderShipTo = Order["shipTo"]`) in the same generated file, and
    parsing recurses to any depth: coerce mode coerces nested fields (and builds
    deep defaults for non-object input), strict mode throws path-aware errors
    like `[OrderShipTo] field "zip" expected string, got number`.
  - **`additionalProperties: false` is enforced.** Strict mode throws
    `[TypeName] unknown property "key"`; coerce mode strips undeclared keys from
    the result instead of spreading them through (previously extras — including
    a potential `__proto__` — flowed straight into the typed output). The shape
    predicate and the parser fast path refuse inputs with undeclared keys so
    extras cannot survive via `{ ...input }`. The declared-keys Set is hoisted
    to module scope and the sweep is an allocation-free `for...in` loop.

  Schemas without `additionalProperties: false` generate byte-identical output
  to before, so loose parsing keeps its existing fast path. Schemas combining
  `additionalProperties: false` with `patternProperties` or composition keywords
  skip the undeclared-key handling, since the generator cannot evaluate those
  yet. The `strict` option docs and config schemas no longer claim unknown keys
  are always allowed.

### Patch Changes

- Updated dependencies [b0c83e7]
  - @amritk/helpers@0.9.0
## @amritk/generate-validators@0.7.0

### Minor Changes

- cff0369: Generated validators no longer silently skip checks that the runtime
  interpreter performs, closing two correctness gaps:

  - **Inline nested objects are validated recursively.** An object schema written
    directly under `properties` (rather than referenced via `$ref`) previously
    only produced an "is an object" shape check; its fields went completely
    unchecked. The generator now recurses to any depth, reporting errors at the
    correct nested JSON Pointer paths, and `$ref`s buried inside inline nested
    objects are collected as imports.
  - **`additionalProperties: false` is enforced.** Undeclared keys are now
    rejected with the interpreter's `must NOT have additional properties`
    message, at both the root and nested levels. The known-keys Set is hoisted to
    module scope and the sweep uses an allocation-free `for...in` loop, so the
    generated validators stay at Ajv-compiled speed. Schemas combining it with
    `patternProperties` skip the sweep for now, since the generator does not
    evaluate key patterns yet.

  Also fixes array item error paths, which duplicated the property name
  (`/tags/tags/0` instead of `/tags/0`), and updates the README benchmark tables:
  the old throughput numbers were inflated by the skipped nested checks.

  Inputs that previously passed validation against strict or nested schemas may
  now (correctly) fail.

### Patch Changes

- b0c83e7: Fix several correctness issues surfaced by a code review:

  - **yaml**: negative hexadecimal and octal scalars (`-0x10`, `-0o10`) no longer
    have their sign double-applied and flipped positive; out-of-range or malformed
    `\x`/`\u`/`\U` escapes in double-quoted scalars are now treated as literal text
    instead of throwing a `RangeError` (via `String.fromCodePoint`) or silently
    dropping the following characters.
  - **resolve-refs**: `pointerToPath` only coerces canonical RFC 6901 array-index
    tokens to numbers, so a numeric object key with a leading zero such as `"01"`
    is kept as a string rather than aliased to a different key. The shared
    JSON Pointer segment decode is now factored into one helper.
  - **generate-validators**: object/array `const` checks compare with a new
    order-independent `valuesEqual` runtime helper instead of `JSON.stringify`, so
    a reordered-but-equal value matches (in step with the interpreter);
    `propertyNames` now validates every key against the full subschema (length,
    enum, const, `$ref`), not just the `pattern` form; and the draft-04 boolean
    `exclusiveMinimum`/`exclusiveMaximum` form is honored.
  - **helpers**: add `hasStrictExclusiveMinimum` / `hasStrictExclusiveMaximum`
    guards for the draft-04 boolean exclusive-bound form.

- Updated dependencies [b0c83e7]

## `retroglyph-core`

## [0.3.0+retroglyph-core](https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/compare/retroglyph-core-v0.2.1...retroglyph-core-v0.3.0) - 2026-07-23 ### Bug Fixes - [9e4027f]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/9e4027f376023e9ebcf26ff1a2aa3bd0618075a9) *(core)* Mark Color, SystemTheme, and Flow #[non_exhaustive] for consistency with sibling enums by `@matanlurey` in [#361]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/361) > Color, SystemTheme, and Flow were the only public enums lacking > #[non_exhaustive], unlike their siblings (KeyCode, MouseButton, > MouseEventKind, Event, BlendMode). Color in particular is widely matched > downstream, and a future variant (a named/theme color, a 256-palette > split) would otherwise be a breaking change to add. > > Internal exhaustive matches on Color that needed a wildcard arm to keep > compiling: > - crates/software/src/lib.rs: resolve_color (falls back to default_rgb) > - crates/terminal/src/lib.rs: write_sgr_params (falls back to the reset > code, same as Color::Default) > > crates/core/src/app.rs's run loop's match on Flow was converted to an > equality check against Flow::Exit (clippy single_match), so any future > Flow variant is treated as Flow::Continue rather than exiting. > > SystemTheme's doc comment previously argued for staying exhaustive > (exactly two variants can ever be reported by winit/browser APIs); it's > been updated to note the #[non_exhaustive] marker is for consistency > with sibling enums rather than an expectation of a near-term third > variant. > > Per AGENTS.md's breaking-change policy, no ! on this commit -- these are > ordinary API-signature breaks that cargo-semver-checks/release-plz > detect and version-bump on their own. > > Closes #267 - [678298e]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/678298e0fee4bb73d701491b32d0ee92ecca5c58) *(core)* Saturating add for blit destination coordinates by `@matanlurey` in [#351]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/351) > blit/blit_alpha computed the destination coordinate as dst_x/dst_y + (offset > from src_rect origin), where the subtraction saturated but the addition did > not. A destination origin near u16::MAX could wrap the addition, either > landing on the wrong cell (if the wrapped value happened to be in-bounds) or > being rejected by put_tile's bounds check only by luck. > > Switch both computations (in blit and blit_alpha) to saturating_add, matching > the saturating-math convention already used elsewhere in this crate > (from_charmap's height.saturating_add(1), write_grapheme's > x.saturating_add(1)). Saturating to u16::MAX is always caught by the > existing >= dst_width/dst_height bounds check, since a valid index must be > strictly less than a u16-derived dimension. > > Adds unit tests for both blit and blit_alpha with a destination origin near > u16::MAX chosen so the unfixed wrapping add would land in-bounds, asserting > the write is skipped instead, plus a sanity test that ordinary > non-overflowing blits are unaffected. > > Closes #268. - [1ec40a8]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/1ec40a835bdb571e1ae0a207fc933e6d54cc2ad6) *(examples)* Fix wasm-terminal entry macro after Backend/Output/Input/Cursor split by `@matanlurey` in [#339]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/339) > fix(examples, core): fix wasm-terminal example entry macro and stale Backend doc refs > > The #265 Backend/Output/Input/Cursor trait split left two call > sites in examples/src/wasm_entry.rs using UFCS `Backend::set_cursor_visible` > / `Backend::resize`, which no longer compile since `Backend` now has no > methods of its own (it's a pure Output+Input+Cursor bundle). This path is > gated on the wasm-terminal example feature + wasm32 target, so > `cargo test --all-features --workspace` on a host target never compiled it; > only the Docs workflow's WASM example build caught it, breaking main's Docs > job after PR #337 merged. > > Also updates three remaining doc-comment mentions of `Backend::draw_layers`/ > > `Backend::composites_layers` in software/core bench file docs that the #265 > docs sweep missed. > > Verified with tools/build-wasm-examples.sh (all examples, all three > Headless/Terminal/Software WASM variants) and `just check`. - [fda7303]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/fda7303d7e2031d607635848b9ad0823302b04b3) *(window)* Automatically present the terminal after each windowed frame by `@matanlurey` in [#353]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/353) ### Refactor - [c6f36d7]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/c6f36d7bdf320b10cca5d3df9d71d97620852297) *(core)* Split Backend into Output/Input/Cursor facets by `@matanlurey` in [#331]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/331) > * refactor(core): split Backend into Output/Input/Cursor facets > > Splits the fused Backend trait into three independent sibling traits with > no supertrait relationship: Output (draw/draw_layers/flush/size/clear/resize, > the only fallible facet), Input (poll_event/push_event, push_event defaults > to a no-op), and Cursor (set_cursor_visible/set_cursor_position, both default > to a no-op). Backend becomes a pure ergonomic bundle: > > pub trait Backend: Output + Input + Cursor {} > impl Backend for T {} > > so every existing B: Backend generic call site (Terminal, App::step, > layout::render, every widget) keeps compiling unchanged. Headless now > implements Output/Input/Cursor separately instead of one impl Backend. > > Also fixes stray doc/grid/terminal references to crate::Backend::* methods > that moved to Output/Input, and updates the workspace README's backend > overview. > > * refactor(crossterm): implement Output/Input/Cursor instead of fused Backend > > Crossterm now implements Output (draw/flush/size/clear/resize, propagating > std::io::Error), Input (real poll_event; push_event uses the new trait > default since crossterm reads its own event stream), and Cursor (real > escape-code-based show/hide and move) instead of one impl Backend. Updates > crate docs, tests, and benches that referenced Backend::* methods directly > on a concrete Crossterm to import Output/Input instead (bundle-trait > method resolution only works through a generic B: Backend bound, not a > concrete type). > > * refactor(window): fold Presenter into an Output supertrait > > Presenter is now `pub trait Presenter: Output`, dropping its duplicated > draw/draw_layers/needs_full_frame/composites_layers/flush/size/clear/resize > signatures (inherited from Output) and its own Error associated type (also > inherited); Presenter keeps only SurfaceError plus the surface lifecycle > (init_surface/resize_surface/present/cell_size). WindowBackend > now implements Output by delegating to P, Input via its own event queue, and > Cursor via the trait's no-op default (confirmed this matches the prior > fused-Backend impl's cursor methods, which were already no-ops for the > windowed family -- a straight split, not a behavior change). Updates crate > docs (lib.rs architecture diagram, presenter.rs's stale "mirrors the output > half" doc comment, README) and the winit test/doctest presenter stubs to > implement Output + Presenter separately. > > * refactor(software): implement Output/Input/Cursor, drop duplicate Presenter forwarding > > SoftwareRenderer now implements Output, Input, and Cursor directly instead > of one impl Backend. Since retroglyph-window's Presenter is now an Output > supertrait, SoftwareRenderer's own Output impl already satisfies > Presenter: Output, so the old impl retroglyph_window::Presenter block > (which duplicated draw/draw_layers/flush/size/clear/resize by forwarding > through ::method, specifically to keep Presenter out of > scope and avoid method-resolution ambiguity) is deleted; the new Presenter > impl only defines SurfaceError, init_surface, resize_surface, present, and > cell_size. Updates crate/module docs and the benches that called > draw/draw_layers directly on a concrete SoftwareRenderer to import Output > instead of Backend. > > * refactor(terminal-wasm): implement Output/Input/Cursor instead of fused Backend > > TerminalWasm now implements Output (ANSI-emitting draw/flush/clear/resize), > Input (real push_event/poll_event, since this backend is entirely > push-driven), and Cursor (real escape-code cursor show/hide/move) instead of > one impl Backend. Updates doc comment links (Backend::draw/clear/etc. -> > Output::/Input::/Cursor::) and the event-throughput bench's Backend as _ > import to Input as _. > > * fix(terminal-wasm): import Output for wasm32-gated resize call > > The wasm32-only wasm_terminal_resize FFI export imported the old fused > Backend trait to call resize(); after the Output/Input/Cursor split that > method lives on Output. This module is #[cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")], so > cargo test --all-features never compiled it -- only just test-wasm > (wasm-pack test) exercises this path, and CI caught it as a build failure > on PR #331. > > * docs(workspace): update Backend/Presenter references after the trait split > > Sweeps remaining prose describing Backend as a single fused > output+input+cursor trait: the workspace README's backend overview, the > retroglyph-terminal crate's doc comment linking to the old > Backend::draw method (now Output::draw), and docs/testing.md's reference to > Backend::push_event (now Input::push_event). - [98b5f3a]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/98b5f3a6ef11ef1854e29dfbb280ee93b1bc4006) *(crossterm)* Option-based event conversion, fix mouse drag/scroll mapping by `@matanlurey` in [#337]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/337) - [9187baf]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/9187baf83c3a4e4decc3f05e644730c6ac97ac35) *(workspace)* Move benchmarks to per-crate crates/*/benches directories by `@matanlurey` in [#317]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/317) > Replaces the single top-level retroglyph-benches crate with Cargo's standard > per-crate benches/ convention (starting with crates/core/benches/grid_diff.rs). > We're about to add benchmarks for every backend/widgets crate (issues #269, > #275, #285, #292, #307, #316); a shared crate would otherwise accumulate every > crate's dev-dependencies and bench targets in one place instead of living next > to the code each bench measures. > > - Move benches/benches/grid_diff.rs -> crates/core/benches/grid_diff.rs and its > [[bench]] entry + dev-dependencies (criterion, fastrand) into > crates/core/Cargo.toml. Drop the now-empty retroglyph-benches crate and its > workspace member entry. > - just bench, tools/bench-compare.sh, and .github/workflows/bench.yml now run > `cargo bench --workspace --all-features` (no -p), so a uniquely-named bench > target resolves regardless of which crate owns it. --all-features matches > just test's convention and avoids a pre-existing retroglyph-software > default-features gap (missing default-font) that only surfaces once the > whole workspace builds in bench/test profile together. > - Update CONTRIBUTING.md, codecov.yml's ignore globs, and Cargo.toml's > comments to match. ### Documentation - [81d2e1b]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/81d2e1b485d23006ec31505625a2315cab0d4727) *(core)* Clarify draw's egc-only grapheme field by `@matanlurey` in [#332]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/332) ### Performance - [8b7cc7a]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/8b7cc7a88e37ec6f159f05bb1cecd95d7fd33737) *(core)* Reduce Grid's layer-table footprint for typical single/few-layer use by `@matanlurey` in [#359]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/359) > perf(core): lazily grow Grid's layer table instead of pre-allocating all 256 slots > > Grid::new previously called layers.resize_with(256, || None) unconditionally, so > every Grid carried a 256-element Vec> (16,384 bytes -- 256 * 64 > bytes per Option, measured via size_of) even for single-layer use. > Terminal holds up to four Grids (current, previous, flattened_current, > flattened_previous), so this was 65,536 bytes of always-allocated, mostly-null > layer table per Terminal. > > Grid::new now starts the layer table at a single slot (layer 0, always > allocated). layer_or_alloc grows the Vec via resize_with up to id + 1 only when > a layer is first written to. Reads of an id beyond the table's current length > return None via a bounds check (Vec::get) instead of indexing directly, with > identical semantics to an in-bounds None slot. max_layer tracking, clear, > clear_all, diff, and flatten_into are unaffected: they already walk > 0..=max_layer or self.layers.iter_mut().flatten(), both of which are correct > over a shorter Vec. > > Added crates/core/benches/grid_construct.rs to measure Grid::new's construction > cost before/after (see PR body for numbers), and unit tests covering lazy growth > to the written id, monotonic growth across writes, and out-of-bounds reads/ > clears behaving like in-bounds None slots. > > Closes #264 - [d30b1c1]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/d30b1c1281f0f64639293d8e7942fa366a575844) *(core)* Flat-iteration flatten_into and blit/blit_alpha by `@matanlurey` in [#338]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/338) - [6ae4219]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/6ae4219b9bd7c066d40051bc9fa4c247d9e454d2) *(terminal)* Buffered, width-precomputed draw with escape/plain split by `@matanlurey` in [#335]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/335) ### Testing - [0884ca6]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/commit/0884ca6fa26557b6348f4b32abc78f4a6f1314fc) *(core)* Add benchmarks for flatten/blit/subcell/color hot paths by `@matanlurey` in [#322]( https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/pull/322) > Adds criterion benches for the remaining per-frame hot paths flagged in > #269 (grid_diff.rs already covered Grid::diff): > > - flatten.rs: Grid::flatten_into at 1/4/16 layers, driven through > Terminal::present (flatten_into is crate-private) since Headless never > overrides composites_layers. > - blit.rs: Grid::blit and Grid::blit_alpha (each BlendMode) over a large > rect (80x24 and 200x60). > - subcell.rs: quantize_half_block/quantize_quadrant/quantize_sextant over > batches of random pixel blocks. > - color.rs: Color::to_indexed (the gem 256-color quantizer), Color::lerp, > and the non-Linear BlendModes via blit_alpha on a 1x1 grid (blend_color > itself is crate-private, so blit_alpha is the only public entry point > that reaches it). > > All inputs use fastrand::Rng::with_seed(42) (or another fixed seed) for > deterministic, --baseline-comparable runs, following grid_diff.rs's > existing style. Each bench group sets criterion::Throughput::Elements to > report cells/blocks/colors-touched alongside time, per the issue's ask > for regressions in output size (not just speed) to stay visible. > > Closes #269 **Full Changelog**: https://github.com/crates-lurey-io/retroglyph/compare/retroglyph-core-v0.2.1...retroglyph-core-v0.3.0

items.title: Portfolio polish: address external review and ship the real PyFlink detector
items.body:
## Summary

Phase A of the post-grading polish plan. Closes the gaps the external reviewer
flagged in `/tmp/review/phishing-radar-review.md` and replaces the deployed
`python_detector.py` chapuza with the actual PyFlink job. Seventeen commits,
one idea each, on top of `main`.

## What's in here

**Honesty in the README**
- `docs(readme): add Known limitations section` — at-least-once delivery, detection latency floor, CT firehose loss, single-instance services, brand allowlist scope, GeoLite2 accuracy, detector horizontal scaling, Streamlit cache window.
- `docs(readme): document latency, throughput and backpressure` — concrete numbers per hop, observed throughput, no-circuit-breaker call-out.
- `build: pin dependency tree via uv.lock and document the rationale` — `just setup` runs `uv sync --frozen`.

**dbt and CI**
- `test(dbt): assert unique on mart_c2_active.ip_address`
- `feat(dbt): freshness thresholds on streaming and batch sources` — `dbt source freshness` flags silent Kestra failures.
- `ci: run dbt test and source freshness on every PR` — was only `dbt parse`.
- `ci(deploy): gate Fly deploys behind a production environment approval` — requires the `production` GitHub environment with at least one required reviewer.

**Batch ingesters**
- `feat(batch): retry/backoff on every ingester HTTP fetch` — `http_session()` with `urllib3 Retry` (5 attempts, 0.5–8 s exponential backoff).
- `test(batch): unit tests for every ingester parser plus http_session` — 7 new tests with mocked HTTP responses.

**Container hygiene**
- `build(docker): multi-stage builds with non-root runtime user` — `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.kestra` both.

**Streaming**
- `feat(detector): externalise brand list to YAML loaded by env var` — `STREAMING_BRAND_LIST_PATH`, default points at `streaming/flink/brands.yaml`.
- `refactor(dashboard): tier the Streamlit cache TTLs by data cadence` — `LIVE_TTL=60`, `BATCH_TTL=300`, `FILTER_TTL=600`.
- `feat(sink): watchdog thread that exits on consumer freeze` — fixes the silent freeze we hit on 2026-04-27.
- `perf(sink): cap fetch budget so multi-topic poll rotates fairly` — `fetch.max.bytes=4MB`.
- `feat(producer): enable idempotent Kafka producer` — `enable.idempotence=true` plus the librdkafka prerequisites.

**Observability**
- `docs(memory): observed RSS peaks, sizing rationale and memray recipes` — `docs/memory_profile.md`, `just profile-{producer,detector,sink}`, includes the `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` / librdkafka cautionary tale.

**The big one**
- `feat(detector): swap deployed binary to the PyFlink MiniCluster job` — `Dockerfile.detector` (Python 3.11 over eclipse-temurin:17-jre + apache-flink installed inside the venv), `deploy/detector/fly.toml` bumped to 1024 MB and pointed at the new dockerfile, `python_detector.py` retained as `just detect-no-java` for quick local iteration without a JDK. README and Mermaid updated.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest` — 27/27 (was 19, plus 7 batch tests, plus 1 brand-loader test).
- [x] `ruff check .` — clean.
- [x] `mypy batch/ streaming/ tests/` — no new errors over the pre-existing baseline.
- [ ] First deploy to Fly: validate Dockerfile.detector image builds and the PyFlink MiniCluster boots inside the 1 GB VM.
- [ ] Configure the `production` GitHub environment with a required reviewer before relying on the gate.
- [ ] Watch `just dbt-freshness` once: should stay green while batch keeps loading.

items.title: fix(elasticsearch): disable periodic refresh during bulk upload, matching OpenSearch and upstream (Closes #240)
items.body:
Closes #240.

## The measurement first — including the part that did not go as predicted

`elasticsearch.rs` created its index with `refresh_interval: "10s"`; `opensearch.rs` uses `-1`, and upstream qdrant uses `-1` for Elasticsearch too (`engine/clients/elasticsearch/configure.py`: *"no refresh is required because we index all the data at once"*). This PR sets ES to `-1` and adds the explicit `_refresh` that visibility then depends on.

Measured live against `tests/docker-compose.test.yml`'s Elasticsearch 9.4.3 on `:9201`, 400,000 × 64d cosine vectors, `elasticsearch-default` (m=16, ef_construction=100, 16 upload threads), A/B **order-alternated**, both arms the same binary except for this diff. Server counters are sampled between the *"Starting upload"* and *"Upload time:"* markers, so they cover exactly the ingest window.

| rep | arm | upload s | ES container CPU s | refreshes | refresh ms | segments left for the merge | host 1-min load |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **new** (`-1`) | 209.1 | 641.6 | 3 | 9120 | 68 | 71.3 |
| 1 | old (`10s`) | 132.2 | 488.1 | 13 | 15412 | 123 | 49.5 |
| 2 | old | 74.1 | 472.3 | 8 | 7568 | 115 | 39.2 |
| 2 | **new** | 114.0 | 559.6 | 1 | 1212 | 38 | 35.2 |
| 3 | **new** | 60.0 | 457.1 | 2 | 986 | 67 | 21.0 |
| 3 | old | 70.3 | 493.0 | 8 | 3727 | 117 | 27.4 |
| 4 | old | 78.1 | 490.4 | 8 | 6372 | 112 | 31.9 |
| 4 | **new** | 97.1 | 543.7 | 1 | 2979 | 42 | 38.1 |
| 5 | **new** | 165.6 | 572.5 | 2 | 5365 | 46 | 47.4 |
| 5 | old | 76.8 | 505.9 | 8 | 5798 | 112 | 30.9 |
| 6 | old | 74.0 | 493.7 | 8 | 5730 | 115 | 30.1 |
| 6 | **new** | 77.2 | 523.3 | 1 | 1715 | 47 | 30.6 |
| | **median old** | **75.5** | **491.7** | **8** | **6085** | **115** | |
| | **median new** | **105.6** | **551.6** | **1.5** | **2347** | **46.5** | |

**What is resolvable, in every single paired run:** the old setting made Elasticsearch do **~5x more refreshes** (median 8 vs 1.5), spend **~2.6x more time refreshing** (6.1 s vs 2.3 s), and cut **~2.5x more segments** (115 vs 47) inside the measured upload window. Refresh count and segment count are pure counts — no timing, no contention sensitivity. That work is real, it was charged to our published ES upload number, and neither OpenSearch nor the reference tool pays it.

**What is *not* resolvable, stated plainly:** a wall-clock upload speedup. This box has 14 cores and was running at 1-min load 21–71 from other jobs throughout; the same binary on the same dataset produced upload times from 60.0 s to 209.1 s. The best-matched pair (rep 6, loads 30.1 vs 30.6) has the new arm **4% slower**; rep 3 has it **15% faster**. The between-arm difference sits well inside each arm's own spread. **I am not claiming an upload throughput improvement, because this measurement does not establish one.**

**So: were prior ES upload numbers understated?** #240 predicted yes. **The measurement does not support that, and I would rather say so than ship the number the issue expected.** There is a plausible mechanism for why the sign is not obvious on an HNSW field: frequent refreshes cut many *small* segments, and building k small HNSW graphs over n/k docs each costs `n·log(n/k)` — *cheaper* per document than the few large graphs `-1` produces. The refresh setting moves HNSW construction between the ingest phase and the merge phase more than it removes it. The 100k full-run A/B below shows that shift directly.

The defect this PR actually fixes is therefore **comparability, not throughput**: our ES numbers were produced under a different index configuration than our OpenSearch numbers and than upstream's, so the ES-vs-OS pairing was not apples-to-apples. Published ES upload figures should be treated as *not comparable to OpenSearch's*, not as *too low*.

### Where the work moves (100k × 64d, full upload + refresh + force-merge, alternated)

| rep | arm | upload s | index (refresh+merge) s | total s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | new | 35.7 | 210.3 | 248.7 |
| 1 | old | 45.2 | 159.5 | 209.6 |
| 2 | old | 38.4 | 158.6 | 199.0 |
| 2 | new | 49.8 | 206.4 | 261.4 |
| 3 | new | 54.9 | 187.4 | 248.8 |
| 3 | old | 23.0 | 111.1 | 135.1 |
| 4 | old | 22.4 | 69.4 | 94.7 |
| 4 | new | 10.4 | 162.8 | 173.8 |
| 5 | new | 31.0 | 172.0 | 209.7 |
| 5 | old | 37.5 | 122.8 | 166.6 |

The index phase is longer for `-1` in **5 of 5 pairs**. At this size the 26 MB corpus fits entirely inside ES's index buffer, so with `-1` the ingest cuts *zero* segments and the force-merge builds the whole graph — the extreme of the same shift. Worth knowing before anyone reads a `total_time` regression as a bug. `upload_time` and `total_time` are both recorded in the results JSON.

## Correctness: the documents are still searchable

With no periodic refresh, something has to make the segments visible. The existing force-merge does **not** suffice on its own — it rewrites segments but does not promise to reopen the searcher, and ES's "search idle" auto-refresh escape hatch explicitly does not apply to an index that has an explicit `refresh_interval`. So `upload()` now calls `refresh()` before `force_merge()`, exactly as `opensearch.rs` already does.

Settings read back off the live server (the only proof that matters — `-1` as a JSON number is accepted and stored):

```
$ curl -s "localhost:9201/bench/_settings?filter_path=**.number_of_shards,**.number_of_replicas,**.refresh_interval"
{"bench":{"settings":{"index":{"refresh_interval":"-1","number_of_shards":"1","number_of_replicas":"0"}}}}
```

Full corpus visible to search after every upload, both arms, all four end-to-end runs:

```
$ curl -s localhost:9201/bench/_count
{"count":100000,"_shards":{"total":1,"successful":1,"skipped":0,"failed":0}}
```

### Recall is unchanged

Two full upload+search rounds per arm, order reversed between rounds, `--parallels 1`, `REPETITIONS=1`, exact ground truth computed with numpy:

| num_candidates | old r1 | old r2 | **new r1** | **new r2** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 0.7110 | 0.7370 | **0.7460** | **0.7300** |
| 256 | 0.8840 | 0.8880 | **0.9010** | **0.8740** |
| 512 | 0.9540 | 0.9570 | **0.9570** | **0.9530** |

MRR was 1.0000 in all 12 measurements and NDCG tracks recall. Each arm's own build-to-build spread (old 0.7110–0.7370, new 0.7300–0.7460 at 128) fully contains the between-arm difference — expected, since the final HNSW graph is merged from a different segment structure and is a different valid approximation. No systematic recall change. QPS also moved by more within an arm than between arms on this loaded host, so no search-side claim is made either.

Two further `-1` builds after the `master` merge (below) put the nc=512 build-to-build spread at **0.9390–0.9580** on a single fixed dataset — wider than the 0.9530–0.9570 the four runs above happened to sample, and it contains every value in the table. Recall on an HNSW index is a per-build quantity; that is the right way to read this table.

### Mixed / update workloads

Checked: `ElasticsearchEngine` does not implement `search_mixed` (only `mongodb_engine.rs` and `vectorsets.rs` do) and has no update or streaming path. Nothing after upload depends on a periodic refresh, so leaving `refresh_interval` at `-1` through the search phase is safe. If a mixed ES path is ever added it must re-refresh or set `refresh=wait_for` on its writes — the doc comment on `build_index_settings` says so.

## Changes

1. **`build_index_settings()`** — index settings hoisted out of `create_index` into a free function so they are unit-testable, with `refresh_interval: -1`. Mirrors `opensearch.rs::build_index_settings`.
2. **`ElasticsearchEngine::refresh()`** — explicit `_refresh` before force-merge, on the same 30-attempt retry budget as force-merge (it runs after the whole ingest; failing it un-retried would discard a long upload).
3. **Guard tests** `index_settings_disable_periodic_refresh` and `index_settings_pin_single_shard_no_replicas`.
4. **`tests/integration_elasticsearch.rs`** — the one test that mirrors the engine's production settings now mirrors `-1`. The other ES tests already used `-1` with explicit `_refresh` calls.
5. **memory-bank story 002** — annotated as superseded so the old `"10s"` spec is not re-implemented from the record.

## Relationship to #235 / #211 — now merged, and the conflict resolved

#235 landed as `d4c2177` while this was open, so the two halves are now in one branch. It pinned `number_of_shards` on the shipped OpenSearch configs and extracted `pub(crate) const ES_NUMBER_OF_SHARDS: i64 = 1;` in `elasticsearch.rs`. Shard count was the first half of the apples-to-apples claim; refresh behaviour is the second. Both engines now ingest under matching shard count *and* matching refresh behaviour, so #235's README claim is true rather than aspirational. Same family as #218 (Milvus without scalar indexes) and the pgvector `parallel-maintenance-workers` gap.

`origin/master` (`71cf574`) is merged in (merge commit, no rebase). **One conflict**, in the index-create `json!` body: #235 replaced the inline `"number_of_shards": 1` with the new constant, while this branch hoisted that whole settings object into `build_index_settings()`.

Resolved by keeping both — `build_index_settings()` stays and now sources the shard count from `ES_NUMBER_OF_SHARDS` rather than a literal:

```rust
fn build_index_settings() -> serde_json::Value {
    serde_json::json!({
        // Cross-engine invariant, not a local choice — see the constant's docs.
        "number_of_shards": ES_NUMBER_OF_SHARDS,
        "number_of_replicas": 0,
        "refresh_interval": -1,
    })
}
```

The guard test asserts against `ES_NUMBER_OF_SHARDS`, **not** against `1`, so hoisting cannot silently desynchronise the pairing that `opensearch::tests::shipped_opensearch_configs_pin_their_shard_count` keys off. #241's `shipped_config_knob_guard` is green (this change removes no config keys).

Both live claims re-verified against the merged tree, since neither survives a bad merge automatically:

```
$ curl -s "localhost:9201/bench/_settings?filter_path=**.number_of_shards,**.number_of_replicas,**.refresh_interval"
{"bench":{"settings":{"index":{"refresh_interval":"-1","number_of_shards":"1","number_of_replicas":"0"}}}}
```

— byte-identical to the pre-merge read-back, so the constant still resolves to 1. And the explicit refresh is still in the path ahead of the merge, with the full corpus visible:

```
Upload time: 9.243s (10819 records/sec)
Refreshing index...
Forcing merge into 1 segment...
```

items.title: Tune GLM-5.1 serving after DeepGEMM investigation
items.body:
# Tune GLM-5.1 serving after DeepGEMM investigation

## Summary

This follow-up updates the huge-model serving defaults after the GLM/Kimi sweep:

- Fixes the GLM-5.1 DeepGEMM environment so BF16 GLM can run without `--enforce-eager`, enabling CUDA graphs and improving throughput from ~7.5 tok/s to ~46 tok/s single-request.
- Keeps the existing Kimi-K2.6 serving default unchanged after testing Kimi-K2.5 recipe-inspired variants; `--async-scheduling`, `--mm-encoder-tp-mode data`, and K2.5 Eagle3 did not improve K2.6 on this vLLM 0.19.1 stack.
- Raises Kimi's `max_output_tokens` to 200k after the old 131k cap caused five hard one-shot CritPt problems to stop before emitting parseable answer code.
- Documents why `zai-org/GLM-5.1-FP8` is not the chosen default here: no-eager FP8 repeatedly fails in DeepGEMM FP8 warmup, while eager FP8 serves but is slower than BF16 no-eager.

References used for the sweep:

- GLM vLLM recipe: https://github.com/vllm-project/recipes/blob/main/GLM/GLM5.md
- Kimi-K2.5 vLLM recipe: https://github.com/vllm-project/recipes/blob/main/moonshotai/Kimi-K2.5.md

## Headline Results

Throughput numbers are aggregate output token throughput from the synthetic OpenAI-compatible benchmark used during tuning. "8-way" and "16-way" mean 8 or 16 concurrent requests to the same vLLM endpoint.

| Model/config | Nodes | 1 req | 8-way | 16-way | Verdict |
|--------------|------:|------:|------:|-------:|---------|
| `zai-org/GLM-5.1` BF16, no eager | 3 | ~46 tok/s | ~202 tok/s | ~333 tok/s | New GLM default |
| `zai-org/GLM-5.1` BF16, no eager | 4 | ~46 tok/s | ~257 tok/s | ~383 tok/s | Comparable-to-Kimi run; not GPU-efficient enough for default |
| `zai-org/GLM-5.1-FP8`, eager, MTP=3 | 2 | ~11 tok/s | ~77 tok/s | ~157 tok/s | Too slow |
| `zai-org/GLM-5.1-FP8`, no eager | 2 | n/a | n/a | n/a | Fails DeepGEMM FP8 warmup |
| `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6` canonical | 2 | ~94 tok/s | ~569 tok/s | ~938 tok/s | Fits; best short-prompt cost/perf, limited full-context KV headroom |
| `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6` canonical | 3 | ~92 tok/s | ~547 tok/s | ~920 tok/s | Fits; nearly enough full-context headroom for 8-way |
| `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6` canonical | 4 | ~92 tok/s | ~558 tok/s | ~920 tok/s | Existing default remains best |

The Kimi full CritPt result directory is now complete: `70/70` submission JSONs. It improved from 57/70 to 65/70 via normal retries, then the final five (`C21`, `C26`, `C27`, `C41`, `C52`) completed after increasing Kimi's max output cap to 200k.

## What Changed

- `serve/serve.slurm`
  - Loads `cuda/12.9` as before, then pins DeepGEMM JIT to a writable persistent cache under `HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE` (or the repo-local `.cache` fallback).
  - Exports `DG_JIT_NVCC_COMPILER` from the loaded CUDA toolkit when available.
  - This is the key fix that lets BF16 GLM use the no-eager CUDA graph path.

- `pyproject.toml`
  - GLM installation stays reproducible through `uv sync --extra local`: the `local` extra includes `vllm`, the required `transformers` floor, and `deep-gemm`.
  - `deep-gemm` resolves from the vendored wheel via `[tool.uv.sources]`, so no manual DeepGEMM install is needed for the BF16 GLM default.

- `src/open_dirac/models.yaml`
  - Removes `--enforce-eager` from canonical `zai-org/GLM-5.1`.
  - Updates the GLM and Kimi experiment notes with the latest measurements and dead ends.
  - Raises `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6` `max_output_tokens` from 131072 to 200000.
  - Documents Kimi 2-node and 3-node reduced-resource benchmarks while keeping the robust 4-node default.
  - Removes temporary experiment aliases for Kimi async/mm-data/Eagle3 and GLM FP8 variants.

- `README.md`
  - Replaces the old "GLM not recommended because eager is required" framing.
  - Adds updated throughput tables for GLM BF16, Kimi, and GLM FP8 caveats.
  - Clarifies that `GLM-5.1-FP8` is not the selected config on this environment.

- `tests/test_config.py`
  - Updates the serve-config assertions so tests now pin GLM's no-eager default.

## Validation

- `uv run --no-sync pytest tests/test_config.py`
- Served and benchmarked:
  - GLM-5.1 BF16 no-eager: healthy and generated successfully.
  - GLM-5.1 BF16 no-eager on 4 nodes: healthy, same single-request speed, higher aggregate throughput, worse GPU efficiency than the 3-node default.
  - GLM-5.1-FP8 eager, no MTP / MTP=1 / MTP=3: healthy but slow.
  - GLM-5.1-FP8 no-eager, shared and isolated caches: fails with `CUDA_ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` in DeepGEMM FP8 warmup.
  - Kimi-K2.6 canonical / async / mm-data: healthy, effectively tied.
  - Kimi-K2.6 canonical on 2 and 3 nodes: healthy; short-prompt throughput tied 4 nodes, but full-context KV headroom is lower.
  - Kimi-K2.6 full one-shot CritPt sweep: `70/70` submission JSONs after the 200k output-token retry.
- Cleaned up completed diagnostic Slurm jobs; no open-dirac experiment jobs remain running.

## Notes

The official GLM FP8 recipe likely needs the Docker/source stack from the recipe rather than our current pip wheel plus local DeepGEMM wheel. On the current environment, BF16 GLM no-eager is the practical default.

items.title: Support both load models; default to closed (concurrency sweep)
items.body:
## Why

Every comparable FHIR-server benchmark in the wild uses the **closed model** ("N concurrent users") — including the one HAPI run on a matched 4-vCPU envelope we found ([Medblocks](https://medblocks.com/blog/couchbase-fhir-vs-hapi-fhir-who-is-faster)). To keep our "where we stand" numbers interpretable alongside the field — and because the choice is internally fair either way (we run every server through the same harness) — make the load model configurable and **default to closed**, while keeping **open** available for coordinated-omission-free tail latency.

## What

A single knob `run.load_model: closed | open` (env override `LOAD_MODEL`), threaded through the whole harness:

- **`scenarios/lib/common.js`** — both executors retained (`constant-vus` + `constant-arrival-rate`); `executor()` selects by `LOAD_MODEL`; summary line is model-aware.
- **`read-mix.js` / `ingest.js`** — use `executor()`.
- **`scenarios/run.sh`** — closed: `CONCURRENCY` → `VUS`; open: `RATE` → VU-pool sizing. Exports `LOAD_MODEL` to k6.
- **`bench.config.yaml`** — `load_model: closed` + both `concurrency_levels` (closed) and `rate_levels` (open) per workload.
- **`orchestrator/orchestrate.sh`** — `MODEL` resolved once; `levels_for`/`lvl_env`/`lvl_prefix`/`lvl_label` pick the right ladder / env (`CONCURRENCY=`|`RATE=`) / results dir (`c-N`|`rate-R`) / label; manifest records `load_model` + `levels`.
- **`reporting/report.py`** — reads `load_model` from the manifest and renders the matching report: **throughput-vs-concurrency** (peak + max-under-SLO) for closed, **latency-vs-rate** (max sustainable) for open.
- **`run-detached.sh`** passes `LOAD_MODEL`/`CONCURRENCY_LEVELS`/`RATE_LEVELS` through; **Makefile** + **CI smoke** switch to closed-model concurrency; **docs** (`load-model.md`, `proposal.md` note, READMEs) updated — closed default, open optional.

Internal fairness holds under either model (same harness for every server); the choice only affects CO-honesty of tails (open) vs comparability with published numbers (closed). Under closed we headline throughput (CO-immune) and treat near-saturation tails as indicative.

## Validation

- `bash -n` (run.sh, orchestrate.sh, run-detached.sh); `py_compile report.py`; `make -n smoke`.
- `report.py` run against **both** a synthetic closed-model tree (→ throughput-vs-concurrency, peak 11000 @ C=64, max-under-SLO 9800 @ C=32) and an open-model tree (→ latency-vs-rate, max sustainable 200, 400 excluded on dropped+p99). Both render correctly.
